questions.stem: Which is the caudal dilatation in the primitive heart tube?
questions.why: The sinus venosus forms the caudal inflow end of the straight heart tube. It receives the embryonic venous return and passes it into the primitive atrium.

notes.A: The primitive atrium receives blood from the sinus venosus, placing it just beyond the venous inlet.
notes.B: The bulbus cordis lies at the arterial end and contributes to the developing right ventricle.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle lies between the atrium and bulbus cordis and pumps blood towards the arterial end.
notes.E: The similarly named conus cordis forms ventricular outflow tracts at the arterial end of the tube.

questions.stem: Which is the septum whose development is directly associated with the foramen ovale in the developing heart?
questions.why: The free margin of the septum secundum forms the rim of the foramen ovale. The thinner septum primum overlaps the opening on its left side and acts as its valve.

notes.A: The thin septum primum supplies the mobile flap that covers the opening on its left side.
notes.B: The septum spurium forms where the venous valves meet near the entry of the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The venous valves form the septum spurium, whereas the rim of the opening belongs to the septum secundum.
notes.E: The septum secundum leaves an identifiable opening through which foetal blood passes into the left atrium.

questions.stem: What is the wide diameter channel that connects the left umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava in the foetus?
questions.why: The ductus venosus carries a portion of the relatively oxygen-rich blood from the left umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta so blood can bypass the foetal lungs.
notes.B: The truncus arteriosus is the common arterial outlet of the embryonic heart before the great arteries separate.
notes.C: The sinus venosus receives embryonic venous blood at the heart and has no direct shunting role within the liver.
notes.E: The ductus venosus provides the named connection that allows placental blood to bypass much of the hepatic circulation.

questions.stem: What is the structure that is formed by the fusion of endocardial (atrioventricular) cushions that divide the atrioventricular canal into right and left channels during development of the heart?
questions.why: The dorsal and ventral atrioventricular endocardial cushions fuse in the common canal. The resulting septum intermedium separates the canal into right and left atrioventricular openings.

notes.A: The foramen ovale is a passage between the foetal atria, above the level of the atrioventricular canal.
notes.B: The septum secundum forms the rim of the interatrial opening on the right side of the atrial septum.
notes.C: The septum spurium arises near the venous inlet from the upper ends of the venous valves.
notes.D: The septum primum grows from the atrial roof towards the cushions and helps partition the atria.

questions.stem: In the congenital anomaly of heart development known as Fallot’s tetralogy, ALL of the following defects are present, EXCEPT:
questions.why: Displacement of the outlet septum produces an overriding aorta, a ventricular septal defect and right ventricular outflow obstruction. The increased right ventricular pressure load leads to hypertrophy.

notes.B: The aorta overrides the septal defect, allowing it to receive blood from both ventricles.
notes.C: Displacement of the outlet septum leaves a gap between the ventricles immediately beneath the overriding aorta.
notes.D: The displaced outlet septum narrows the right ventricular outflow tract, restricting flow towards the lungs.
notes.E: The right ventricular muscle becomes hypertrophied as it pumps against the obstruction at its outlet.

questions.stem: Concerning blood circulation in the foetus evaluate the following statements

options.label: A
options.text: Oxygen-rich blood from the placental bed reaches the foetus through umbilical arteries

options.label: B
options.text: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk into the dorsal aorta

options.label: C
options.text: The most oxygen-rich blood flows through the arch of the aorta to the head and upper extremities of the foetus

notes.A: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood towards the foetus, while the paired umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.
notes.C: Among the systemic arteries, the ascending aorta and its arch branches receive relatively oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle.
notes.B: High resistance in the foetal lungs favours flow from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta through the ductus arteriosus.

questions.why: The umbilical vein brings placental blood to the foetus. Preferential streaming across the foramen ovale helps supply the heart and upper body with relatively well-oxygenated arterial blood.

questions.stem: Concerning the septation and development of the primitive atrium into right and left cavities during embryonic life, evaluate the following statements

options.label: A
options.text: The septum primum develops from endocardial cushions

options.label: B
options.text: The septum secundum develops between the septum primum and the septum intermedium

options.label: C
options.text: The foramen ovale forms when the communication between the two halves of the atria becomes an oblique channel

options.label: D
options.text: The septum secundum functions as a flap-like valve

options.label: E
options.text: The septation of the atrial chambers is completed only after birth when the pressure in the right side rises

notes.A: The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium towards the endocardial cushions.
notes.B: The septum secundum develops to the right of the septum primum and overlaps its opening.
notes.C: The openings in the overlapping septa are offset, producing an oblique route from the right atrium to the left.
notes.D: The flexible septum primum opens like a flap against the more substantial septum secundum.
notes.E: Lung aeration increases pulmonary blood flow and left atrial pressure. Functional closure occurs when left pressure exceeds right, and anatomical fusion can lag or remain incomplete.

questions.why: Overlapping atrial septa create an oblique right-to-left passage. Once pulmonary venous return increases at birth, higher left atrial pressure holds the flexible septum primum against the rim.

questions.stem: Evaluate the following statements with respect to the formation of the ventricles during embryonic development

options.label: A
options.text: The primary interventricular septum forms when the endocardial heart tube folds

options.label: B
options.text: The muscular interventricular septum develops from the bulbar ridges

options.label: C
options.text: The membranous part of the interventricular septum forms in part from the endocardial cushions

options.label: D
options.text: The left ventricle forms mainly from the primitive ventricle of the heart tube.

options.label: E
options.text: Interventricular septal defects commonly occur in the membranous part of the interventricular septum

notes.A: Looping positions the cardiac chambers, whereas growth of the ventricular myocardium produces the muscular septum.
notes.B: The muscular septum arises at the floor of the developing ventricles as their walls expand.
notes.C: Tissue from the atrioventricular cushions helps close the remaining gap above the muscular septum.
notes.E: The membranous region is a common site of defects because several developing structures must unite there.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle gives rise to the trabeculated portion that forms most of the left ventricle.

questions.why: Expansion of the ventricular chambers produces the muscular septum and initially leaves an interventricular opening. The cushions and neighbouring outflow tissues help close the remaining gap.

questions.stem: About development of the great arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: The common carotid artery comes from the 3rd aortic arch artery.

options.label: B
options.text: The pulmonary arteries come from the 5th aortic arch artery.

options.label: C
options.text: The distal part of the left 6th arch artery forms the ductus arteriosus.

options.label: D
options.text: The ascending aorta comes from the truncus arteriosus.

options.label: E
options.text: The brachiocephalic artery comes from the aortic sac.

notes.A: The third arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal part of the internal carotid artery on each side.
notes.B: The proximal sixth arch arteries contribute to the pulmonary arteries on their respective sides.
notes.E: The right horn of the aortic sac gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk.
notes.C: The distal left sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, joining the left pulmonary artery to the descending aorta.
notes.D: Partition of the truncus arteriosus produces the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk.

questions.why: The outflow tract separates into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Remodelling of the aortic sac and pharyngeal arch arteries then establishes their connections with the great vessels.

questions.stem: Hours after the birth of a baby boy, the observant mother noticed that he became cyanotic anytime he cried vigorously. What is the embryological explanation and prognosis for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: There has been a coarctation of the baby’s aorta

options.label: B
options.text: Vigorous crying opens a patent ductus venosus

options.label: C
options.text: Vigorous crying increases the pressure in the right atrium that temporary opens a yet-to-fuse septum primum

options.label: D
options.text: Surgery is required to correct the defect causing the problem

options.label: E
options.text: Survival rate is very high for babies with this condition

notes.A: Coarctation gives persistent signs (e.g. weak, delayed femoral pulses), not cyanosis only on crying.
notes.B: The ductus venosus is a shunt within the liver; it cannot mix blood between the atria.
notes.C: The septum primum flap has not yet fused with the septum secundum, so a rise in right atrial pressure opens it and shunts blood right to left.
notes.D: Left atrial pressure normally keeps the flap shut until it fuses, so surgery is rarely needed.
notes.E: The flap usually fuses within the first months of life, so survival is excellent.

questions.why: Crying raises right atrial pressure and pushes open an unfused septum primum flap (a probe-patent foramen ovale), shunting deoxygenated blood to the left side; it usually seals on its own, so the outlook is excellent.

questions.stem: Which fetal blood vessel undergoes fibrosis after birth to form the ligamentum teres hepatis in the falciform ligament of the liver?
questions.why: The intra-abdominal left umbilical vein closes after birth and its fibrous remnant becomes the round ligament of the liver. It runs along the free margin of the falciform ligament.

notes.A: The distal umbilical arteries become the paired medial umbilical ligaments, which run beside the bladder on the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.B: The ductus arteriosus closes and forms the ligamentum arteriosum between the left pulmonary artery and the aortic arch.
notes.C: The ductus venosus closes and forms the ligamentum venosum within the liver, beyond the course of the former umbilical vein.
notes.E: The vitelline veins form parts of the portal venous system and the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava.

questions.stem: Which structure in the fetal heart acts as a flap valve allowing blood to pass from the right atrium to the left atrium?
questions.why: The thin septum primum forms the flap on the left side of the foramen ovale. Raising left atrial pressure presses the flap against the stiffer septum secundum.

notes.A: Endocardial cushions help partition the atrioventricular canal, whereas the flap comes from the septum growing down from the atrial roof.
notes.B: The crista dividens is a ridge that separates incoming blood streams at the rim of the interatrial opening.
notes.D: The septum secundum provides the rim against which the thinner flap closes when left atrial pressure rises.
notes.E: The inferior caval valve helps direct blood towards the foramen ovale from the venous inlet upstream of the flap.

questions.stem: Which of the following veins does NOT contribute to the formation of the inferior vena cava?
questions.why: The umbilical veins never form part of the IVC.

notes.A: A small caudal part.
notes.B: Prerenal part.
notes.C: Postrenal part.
notes.E: Hepatic part.

questions.stem: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form leaves:
questions.why: Failure of embryonic outflow tract separation leaves one common arterial trunk supplying systemic and pulmonary circulations. It usually overrides a large ventricular septal defect.

notes.A: Tetralogy of Fallot involves an abnormally positioned outlet septum, with pulmonary outflow obstruction and an overriding aorta.
notes.B: In transposition there are two separate great arteries, but each connects to the opposite ventricle.
notes.D: A ventricular septal defect is an opening between the ventricles. It often accompanies a common arterial trunk.
notes.E: A patent ductus arteriosus connects an already separate pulmonary artery and aorta through a persistent foetal vessel.

questions.stem: Which primary germ layer (s) give(s) origin to the laryngotracheal bud that gives rise to the respiratory system
questions.why: The laryngotracheal bud grows out from ventral foregut endoderm. Its endoderm forms respiratory epithelium, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm gives rise to supporting cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue.

notes.A: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, whereas the respiratory bud arises within the endoderm-lined foregut.
notes.C: Splanchnic mesoderm around the bud forms bronchial cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue around the endodermal lining.
notes.D: Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall and contributes to the parietal pleura surrounding each lung.
notes.E: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures outside the embryo, including placental vessels, whereas the lung bud forms within the embryo.

questions.stem: A newborn baby was becoming cyanotic within hours of birth, and it was noted that its thorax was becoming gradually distended with every breath as it inhaled but could not exhale air. What is responsible for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: The lungs are hypoplastic owing to oligohydramnios

options.label: B
options.text: The baby has hyaline membrane disease resulting from lack of surfactant

options.label: C
options.text: There is unilateral agenesis of the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: There is neonatal lobar emphysema on account of failure of development of bronchial cartilage

options.label: E
options.text: There is tracheoesophageal fistula compounded by accessory lung lobes

questions.why: An affected lobar bronchus can narrow during expiration when its cartilaginous support is inadequate. Trapped air progressively overinflates the lobe and can compress adjacent functional lung.

notes.A: Oligohydramnios can limit lung growth, leaving small lungs with insufficient tissue for gas exchange.
notes.B: Surfactant deficiency increases surface tension and promotes alveolar collapse at the end of expiration.
notes.C: Unilateral agenesis leaves an entire lung absent and cannot account for air trapping within a developing lobe.
notes.E: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula can permit aspiration or gastric distension. An extra lobe alone supplies no mechanism for focal expiratory air trapping.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the result of imperfect fusion of the margins of the laryngotracheal tube
questions.why: The ventral respiratory diverticulum normally separates from the dorsal oesophagus during foregut development. Abnormal separation can leave a fistula between the trachea and oesophagus.

notes.B: Congenital lobar overinflation results from expiratory air trapping, sometimes because an affected bronchus lacks adequate cartilage.
notes.C: Congenital lung cysts arise within the developing airways or lung tissue, away from the tracheo-oesophageal partition.
notes.D: Hyaline membrane disease arises when surfactant deficiency allows alveoli to collapse, usually in a premature infant.
notes.E: Accessory lung lobes result from variations in branching or lobulation within the developing lung.

questions.stem: Concerning lung development and function, as well as medico-legal cases, evaluate the following

options.label: A
options.text: Lungs from a newborn baby who died before birth will float when placed in water

options.label: B
options.text: Lungs of newborn who died after birth will sink when placed in water

options.label: C
options.text: The lungs are totally non-functional in the foetus

options.label: E
options.text: Respiratory distress syndrome results from lack of surfactant-secreting cells in the epithelium of the lungs

options.label: F
options.text: Congenital lobar emphysema results from lack of pneumocyte type I cells in the epithelium of the lungs

notes.A: Unaerated lungs sink.
notes.B: Aerated lungs float.
notes.C: They secrete fluid and make breathing movements.
notes.D: Alveoli increase until about 8 years.
notes.E: Immature type II cells make too little surfactant.

questions.why: Lung development continues for years after birth and respiratory distress syndrome results from surfactant deficiency (D, E true). A and B are false (an unbreathed lung sinks while a breathed lung floats - the basis of the hydrostatic test), C is false (the fetal lung does secrete fluid and surfactant and makes breathing movements, though it performs no gas exchange) and F is false (congenital lobar emphysema is due to deficient bronchial cartilage, not lack of pneumocytes).

questions.stem: Evaluate the following statements concerning the problems of a baby born with communication between the trachea and oesophagus

options.label: A
options.text: Air will be forced into the stomach when the child cries

options.label: B
options.text: Acidic stomach contents may be forced up the oesophagus through the communication into the trachea and down into the lungs

options.label: C
options.text: Shortly after birth, there will be over-distension of one or more lobes of the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: Surgery is required to repair the fistula

notes.C: Focal lobar overinflation suggests an obstructed bronchus, whereas an open fistula primarily predisposes to aspiration.
notes.A: With a distal fistula, raised airway pressure during crying can drive air through the oesophagus into the stomach.
notes.B: Refluxing gastric contents can travel up the distal oesophagus and through the fistula, causing aspiration and lung injury.
notes.D: Surgical closure separates the airway and digestive tract and prevents continued passage of material through the fistula.

questions.why: An abnormal tract between trachea and oesophagus permits cross-flow. With a distal fistula, airway pressure can inflate the stomach and gastro-oesophageal reflux can enter the airway.

questions.stem: Which membranes that grow over the lung buds and partition the thoracic cavity separate the heart and lungs?
questions.why: Pleuropericardial folds grow medially and separate the pleural spaces from the pericardial cavity. Their fusion helps form the fibrous pericardial partition around the heart.

notes.B: The pleuroperitoneal folds help close communications between the developing pleural and peritoneal cavities and contribute to the diaphragm.
notes.C: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, but the partitions that separate it from the pleural cavities develop as named folds.
notes.D: The dorsal mesentery suspends the developing gut from the posterior body wall within the abdomen.
notes.E: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm between the thorax and abdomen.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the hindgut includes ALL of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Inferior half of the anal canal

options.label: B
options.text: Superior half of the anal canal

questions.why: The pectinate line marks the junction between upper anal canal epithelium derived from hindgut endoderm and the lower segment derived from ectoderm of the proctodeum.

notes.B: The epithelium above the pectinate line is derived from hindgut endoderm and is continuous with the rectal lining.
notes.C: The left colic flexure lies at the transition to descending colon within the distal transverse colon and hindgut territory.
notes.D: The descending colon is formed by the hindgut and is supplied by branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.
notes.E: The sigmoid colon forms from distal hindgut and continues into the rectum, another hindgut derivative.

questions.stem: Which is the wedge of mesenchyme that grows inferiorly to divide the allantois from the hindgut?
questions.why: The urorectal septum is the intervening mesenchyme at the cloaca. It separates the ventral urogenital sinus, continuous with the allantois, from the dorsal anorectal canal.

notes.A: The proctodeum is a surface ectodermal depression that contributes the lower anal canal below the pectinate line.
notes.C: The cloaca is the common terminal chamber being partitioned. The dividing wedge is mesenchyme within this region.
notes.D: The perineal body forms at the junction between the future anal and urogenital openings, at the caudal end of the partition.
notes.E: The urogenital membrane covers the ventral opening after partition and later breaks down. It is separate from the mesenchymal wedge.

questions.stem: In the early stages of development of the digestive system, the anterior limit of the foregut is formed by which of the following?
questions.why: The buccopharyngeal membrane closes the cranial end of the early foregut. Its breakdown opens a connection between the primitive mouth and the developing pharynx.

notes.A: The yolk sac connects to the midgut through a narrowing stalk. This junction lies caudal to the primitive pharynx.
notes.B: The vitelline duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac. It does not form the cranial limit of the foregut.
notes.C: The cloacal membrane marks the caudal outlet of the hindgut region, at the opposite end of the developing gut tube.
notes.E: The respiratory bud forms from the ventral foregut below the pharynx, caudal to the buccopharyngeal membrane.

questions.stem: ALL of the following develop from the hepatic bud, EXCEPT:
questions.why: The dorsal pancreatic bud arises independently from the dorsal duodenal endoderm. The ventral pancreatic bud, hepatic primordium and gallbladder are associated with the ventral hepatic diverticulum.

notes.B: The ventral pancreatic primordium arises from the ventral foregut near or as part of the developing hepatic diverticulum.
notes.C: The gallbladder develops from the cystic portion of the hepatic diverticulum, caudal to the liver-forming portion.
notes.D: The cystic bud is the portion of the ventral diverticulum that gives rise to the gallbladder and cystic duct.
notes.E: The liver-forming portion of the diverticulum gives rise to hepatic tissue and contributes to the developing biliary tract.

questions.stem: Which of the following events cause congenital oesophageal stenosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of the laryngotracheal tube to bud from the foregut

options.label: B
options.text: Constriction of oesophagus by an excessively large developing lung

options.label: C
options.text: Unequal division of the foregut resulting in a larger laryngotracheal tube

options.label: D
options.text: Incomplete separation of the laryngotracheal tube from the foregut

options.label: E
options.text: Failure of the foregut to be taken into the embryo as it forms the head, tail, and lateral folds

questions.why: Posterior deviation of the tracheoesophageal septum leaves the oesophagus narrow (atresia/stenosis); stenosis also follows faulty recanalization.

notes.A: There would be no lungs.
notes.B: Not a cause.
notes.D: This gives a fistula.
notes.E: Folding failure has other results.

questions.stem: An accessory pancreatic duct develops from which of he following

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow stem of the bud of the gall bladder

questions.why: The accessory pancreatic duct can persist from the dorsal pancreatic duct on the minor-papilla side of the fusion point. The rest joins the main duct system.

notes.A: The stalk of the cystic bud forms the cystic duct, which connects the gallbladder to the extrahepatic bile ducts.
notes.B: The common bile duct carries bile and usually joins the main pancreatic duct near the major papilla.
notes.C: The ventral bud duct forms the outlet portion of the main duct at the major duodenal papilla.
notes.E: The common hepatic duct drains the liver. It joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

questions.stem: A three-month old male baby was brought to a paediatrician because his mother had noticed extrusion of faecal material through the umbilicus. The baby was otherwise perfectly normal. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.why: A completely patent vitelline duct persists as an ileo-umbilical fistula. Its open connection to the bowel lumen allows intestinal contents to discharge through the umbilicus.

notes.A: Meckel’s diverticulum is a blind pouch persisting at the ileal end. It has no open outlet at the umbilicus.
notes.B: A fibrous remnant can tether the ileum to the umbilicus and predispose to obstruction. It lacks an open lumen.
notes.D: A vitelline sinus has a patent umbilical end but closes towards the bowel, so it has no direct faecal communication.
notes.E: A vitelline duct cyst retains a central portion with closed ends. It has no continuous opening between the ileum and skin.

questions.stem: An otherwise perfectly normal baby was born with a hernial sac covered by amnion, and with the umbilical cord attached at the apex. What is your diagnosis?
questions.why: An omphalocoele is a midline herniation into the umbilical cord, usually contained by an amnion-covered sac. The cord inserts into the sac rather than beside it.

notes.A: Gastroschisis usually lies beside the umbilicus. The bowel has no covering sac and the cord inserts separately.
notes.C: A congenital umbilical hernia protrudes through an umbilical ring beneath skin. It lacks the amnion-covered sac described here.
notes.D: Physiological midgut herniation is normal early in development and resolves before birth as bowel returns to the abdomen.
notes.E: An amnion-covered sac with the cord inserting into it is a characteristic anatomical finding in omphalocoele.

questions.stem: A neonatologist diagnosed primary megacolon (Hirschprung’s disease) in a female baby that had failed to pass meconium several hours after birth and had an enormously distended abdomen. The statements below are correct concerning this disease

options.label: B
options.text: There is a higher than average probability that the parents or their siblings may have babies with the same disease

options.label: C
options.text: It is more common in female babies than in males

options.label: D
options.text: The rectum and anal canal in the affected baby are constricted

options.label: E
options.text: A grossly distended pelvic colon is responsible for the intestinal obstruction in the baby

options.label: F
options.text: The constricted segment of the colon is deficient in parasympathetic ganglion cells

options.label: G
options.text: Operative excision of the hypertrophied segment of the colon is the treatment of choice

notes.A: About 2–10% have Down syndrome.
notes.B: Familial.
notes.C: Commoner in boys (4:1).
notes.D: The aganglionic segment is narrow.
notes.E: The obstruction is the aganglionic segment; the proximal colon dilates as a result.

questions.why: Neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon, leaving an aganglionic narrowed segment.

questions.stem: Concerning the development of the pancreas, evaluate the following statements

options.label: A
options.text: The uncinate process develops from the dorsal pancreatic bud

options.label: B
options.text: The lower part of the head of the pancreas develops from the ventral pancreas

options.label: C
options.text: The tail of the pancreas develops from the dorsal pancreatic bud

options.label: D
options.text: The body of the pancreas develops from the ventral pancreatic bud

options.label: E
options.text: The proximal part of the main pancreatic duct derives from the duct of the ventral pancreatic bud

options.label: F
options.text: The distal part of the main pancreatic duct derives from the duct of the dorsal bud.

options.label: G
options.text: When the proximal part of the duct of the dorsal pancreas fails to degenerate it forms an accessory pancreatic duct

options.label: H
options.text: An annular pancreas results from division of the ventral pancreatic bud into two

notes.A: The uncinate process grows from the ventral bud. It hooks behind the superior mesenteric vessels after rotation and fusion.
notes.B: The ventral bud supplies the uncinate process and part of the pancreatic head, particularly its inferior portion.
notes.C: The tail is a dorsal bud derivative and extends towards the spleen as the pancreas develops.
notes.D: The body develops from the dorsal bud along with the tail and part of the head.
notes.E: The main duct segment nearest its duodenal outlet is formed from the ventral bud duct.
notes.F: The body and tail portion of the main duct is formed from the dorsal duct beyond its union with the ventral duct.
notes.G: Persistence of the dorsal duct toward its original duodenal opening can leave an accessory duct at the minor papilla.
notes.H: In one classical model, a bifid ventral bud migrates around both sides of the duodenum and forms a pancreatic ring.

questions.why: The ventral pancreatic bud forms the uncinate process and inferior head. The dorsal bud forms most of the rest, and remodelling of both ducts establishes the definitive drainage pattern.

questions.stem: The following statements are correct concerning congenital pyloric stenosis

options.label: A
options.text: It is caused by hypertrophy of the longitudinal muscle of the pylorus

options.label: B
options.text: An affected baby ejects stomach contents with considerable force

options.label: D
options.text: It is more common in boys than in girls

options.label: E
options.text: There is excessive numbers of autonomic ganglion cells in the pyloric muscle

options.label: F
options.text: There is no effective treatment, and all affected babies die

options.label: G
options.text: Symptoms appear within first three days of birth

notes.A: Hypertrophy predominantly affects the circular smooth muscle. This narrows the pyloric channel and impedes gastric emptying.
notes.B: The stomach contracts against the narrowed outlet, producing forceful vomiting of gastric contents without bile.
notes.C: Reduced passage of feeds into the intestine can decrease stool output and may lead to constipation.
notes.D: The condition is considerably more frequent in male infants, although it can also occur in females.
notes.E: Increased numbers of autonomic ganglion cells are not the defining change. The characteristic lesion is muscular thickening of the pylorus.
notes.F: After fluid and electrolyte correction, pyloromyotomy relieves the obstruction and is generally effective.
notes.G: Presentation is typical several weeks after birth. Although timing varies, the first three days are unusually early.

questions.why: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis results from thickening of the pyloric muscle, especially its circular layer. Gastric outlet narrowing leads to forceful non-bilious vomiting, typically after the first weeks of life.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has intestines protruding through the anterior abdominal wall beside the umbilicus, with no sac and the cord attached normally. About her condition:

options.label: B
options.text: Imperfect development of one of the lateral folds of the embryo caused it

options.label: C
options.text: There is full thickness defect in the abdominal wall through which the intestines protrude

options.label: D
options.text: It is caused by a failure of the physiological hernia of the gut to return into the abdominal cavity

options.label: E
options.text: It is caused by mal-rotation of the loop of the midgut in the umbilical cord

notes.A: An umbilical hernia is skin-covered and lies at the umbilicus itself.
notes.B: Faulty closure of a lateral body fold leaves a defect beside (usually right of) the umbilicus.
notes.C: The defect involves the full thickness of the wall, so the bowel lies free with no covering sac.
notes.D: Failure of the physiological hernia to return gives omphalocele, which is covered by amnion.
notes.E: Malrotation may accompany it but does not cause the wall defect.

questions.why: Gastroschisis is a full-thickness lateral body-wall defect (faulty closure of a lateral fold), so bowel protrudes beside a normally inserted cord with no sac; a sac-covered defect at the cord is omphalocele.

questions.stem: From their developmental origins, it is understandable that ALL the listed parts of the GIT are supplied by the superior mesenteric artery EXCEPT:
questions.why: The foregut–midgut boundary in the duodenum lies near the major papilla. The proximal duodenum is foregut-derived and chiefly supplied from the coeliac system via pancreaticoduodenal branches.

notes.A: The ileum is part of the midgut and receives branches of the superior mesenteric artery through its mesentery.
notes.B: The jejunum is midgut-derived. Jejunal arteries arise from the superior mesenteric artery and form mesenteric arcades.
notes.C: The caecum develops from the midgut loop and receives blood through the ileocolic branch of the superior mesenteric artery.
notes.D: Distal to the major papilla the duodenum is midgut-derived. Inferior pancreaticoduodenal branches arise from the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Gastroschisis and omphalocele are two anomalies of the gastrointestinal tract. What is the distinguishing feature of omphalocele?

options.label: B
options.text: Herniation to the right of umbilicus

questions.why: Omphalocoele has a covering sac containing peritoneum and amnion, with the cord attached to it. Gastroschisis leaves the protruding bowel exposed through a separate defect.

notes.B: A defect just to the right of the umbilicus is typical of gastroschisis. Omphalocoele is centred on the umbilical ring.
notes.C: Both conditions involve the anterior abdominal wall. The covering and relation to the cord distinguish them.
notes.D: A separate, normally inserted cord favours gastroschisis. In omphalocoele the cord inserts into the sac.
notes.E: A lateral defect favours gastroschisis. Omphalocoele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring.

questions.stem: Abdominal contents found in the thorax of a newborn through a posterolateral defect is:
questions.why: A posterolateral diaphragmatic defect is a Bochdalek-type congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Abdominal viscera can enter the thorax through it and limit antenatal development of the adjacent lung.

notes.B: A hiatal hernia allows abdominal contents to pass through the oesophageal hiatus rather than through a posterolateral gap.
notes.C: Midgut malrotation changes the position and fixation of the bowel. It does not itself provide a passage through the diaphragm.
notes.D: Prolapse describes protrusion through an opening in general. The posterolateral diaphragmatic defect identifies a specific hernia at this site.
notes.E: A thoracic stomach describes an organ position. Other viscera may also pass through the same posterolateral diaphragmatic defect.

questions.stem: When a short esophagus develops in a fetus, it results in the stomach being pulled into the thorax causing gastroesophageal reflux disease. What is this condition called?
questions.why: A short oesophagus pulls the stomach up: congenital hiatal hernia.

notes.B: No.
notes.C: No.
notes.D: No.
notes.E: Term sometimes used, but the condition named is hiatal hernia.

questions.stem: All of the following are congenital abnormalities of the oesophagus EXCEPT:
questions.why: A double aortic arch is a vascular ring around the trachea and oesophagus. Any oesophageal narrowing results from external compression by the arteries rather than maldevelopment of the oesophageal wall.

notes.A: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a congenital communication between the developing foregut and respiratory passages.
notes.C: Oesophageal atresia is an interruption of the normal lumen that may leave a blind upper pouch, sometimes with a distal fistula.
notes.D: A congenital oesophageal web or septum can narrow the lumen by projecting into it from the wall.
notes.E: A congenitally short oesophagus can leave the gastro-oesophageal junction unusually high and is a developmental abnormality of the oesophagus.

questions.stem: Which is the most frequent malformation of the gastrointestinal tract?
questions.why: Meckel’s diverticulum is a persistent ileal remnant of the vitelline duct. It is found in roughly two percent of people and is often asymptomatic.

notes.A: Oesophageal atresia is a congenital interruption of the oesophagus and is much less frequent than an incidental Meckel’s diverticulum.
notes.C: Omphalocoele is a relatively uncommon ventral wall defect containing herniated viscera within a sac at the cord insertion.
notes.D: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a recognised cause of gastric outlet obstruction but occurs less frequently than Meckel’s diverticulum.
notes.E: Congenital aganglionosis causes functional obstruction in the distal bowel and is less common than persistent ileal diverticulum.

questions.stem: Which correctly indicates the muscle types formed in the developing esophagus?

options.label: A
options.text: Striated muscle in upper 1/3 and smooth muscle in lower 1/3

options.label: B
options.text: Smooth and striated muscle in lower 1/3

options.label: C
options.text: Smooth muscle in upper 1/3 and striated muscle in lower 1/3

options.label: E
options.text: Smooth muscle in middle 1/3 and mixture in lower 1/3

questions.why: The oesophageal muscularis externa is predominantly skeletal in its upper third and smooth in its lower third. The middle third contains a variable mixture of both.

notes.B: Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle is characteristic of the middle portion. The lower oesophageal wall is predominantly smooth muscle.
notes.C: This reverses the distribution. Striated skeletal muscle is proximal and smooth muscle predominates distally.
notes.D: The upper oesophageal muscularis is predominantly skeletal, continuing from the striated musculature of the pharyngeal region.
notes.E: The middle portion contains a mixture. The distal portion continues as smooth muscle towards the stomach.

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true concerning the oesophagus EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It develops from the foregut and the midgut

options.label: B
options.text: It constricts at the level of T10 vertebra

options.label: C
options.text: Oesophageal wall has skeletal and smooth muscles

options.label: D
options.text: Hiatal hernia causes stomach contents to reflux into oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: It is separated from the trachea by the tracheoesophageal septum

questions.why: The oesophagus develops entirely from dorsal foregut. It lengthens as thoracic organs descend, and its muscular wall changes from skeletal proximally to predominantly smooth muscle distally.

notes.B: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm near vertebral level T10, contributing a normal site of constriction.
notes.C: The muscularis externa contains skeletal muscle proximally, smooth muscle distally and a mixture between these regions.
notes.D: A hiatal hernia can disrupt the normal anti-reflux barrier around the gastro-oesophageal junction and promote reflux.
notes.E: The dorsal oesophagus separates from the ventral respiratory tract during partitioning of the early foregut.

questions.stem: Which of the following events causes congenital oesophageal stenosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Failure of foregut to divide into trachea and oesophagus

questions.why: Incomplete recanalisation is the classical explanation for a membrane or narrowed lumen in the developing oesophagus. Other forms of congenital oesophageal stenosis have different wall abnormalities.

notes.A: Failure of foregut partitioning can leave a tracheo-oesophageal communication. A persistent intraluminal membrane reflects a different developmental process.
notes.C: Stomach rotation changes the orientation of the stomach and associated mesenteries. It does not govern reopening of the oesophageal lumen.
notes.D: Cloacal partition separates the lower anorectal and urogenital channels, far caudal to the developing oesophagus.
notes.E: Complete failure of separation would leave a common foregut passage. This differs from a narrowed lumen within a separate oesophagus.

questions.stem: Which condition is common in a newborn baby with either imperforate anus or congenital aganglionic colon?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure to pass meconium within 24–48 hours after birth

questions.why: Both an imperforate anus and distal aganglionosis can prevent the normal early passage of meconium. One obstructs the outlet structurally and the other obstructs it functionally.

notes.B: Forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting is characteristic of gastric outlet obstruction, especially infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
notes.C: Bilious vomiting can accompany intestinal obstruction, but delayed or absent meconium is the more characteristic shared initial clue here.
notes.D: Poor feeding can accompany neonatal illness generally. It does not localise an abnormality of the distal bowel or outlet.
notes.E: Explosive stool can follow rectal examination in Hirschsprung disease with a patent anus. It is not the typical shared presentation.

questions.stem: Which part of the pancreas is formed by the ventral pancreatic bud during embryonic development?
questions.why: The ventral pancreatic bud rotates behind the duodenum and fuses with the dorsal bud. It forms the uncinate process and inferior portion of the head.

notes.A: The pancreatic neck derives mainly from the dorsal bud. It joins the head to the body in the mature gland.
notes.B: The body is derived from the dorsal pancreatic bud, which forms the bulk of the definitive gland.
notes.C: The tail develops from the dorsal bud and extends leftward in the direction of the spleen.
notes.E: Ventral derivatives are limited to the uncinate process and part of the head. The other listed regions are chiefly dorsal.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly explains how an annular pancreas may form during embryonic development?

options.label: A
options.text: Dorsal pancreatic bud that incorrectly rotates to the left

options.label: B
options.text: Ventral pancreatic bud that develops from the hepatic bud and rotates abnormally

options.label: C
options.text: Ventral pancreatic bud that splits into two, with each half rotating in opposite directions

options.label: D
options.text: Duodenum develops too close to the ventral pancreatic bud and compresses it

options.label: E
options.text: One bud remains in common with dorsal pancreas and fails to rotate to the left opposite directions

questions.why: In the classical bifid-bud model, ventral pancreatic tissue passes on both sides of the duodenum and unites dorsally, leaving a ring that can narrow the lumen.

notes.A: The dorsal bud forms the bulk of the pancreas. In this model, tissue of ventral origin surrounds the duodenum.
notes.B: Abnormal ventral development is relevant, but a single unspecified rotation does not explain the classical two-limb mechanism.
notes.D: A duodenal obstruction can result from a pancreatic ring. Compression of the bud by a nearby duodenum does not create that ring.
notes.E: Failure of bud fusion or duct union can leave separate drainage pathways. It does not describe circumferential pancreatic tissue.

questions.stem: From its developmental origin, the arterial supply of the intra-abdominal gastrointestinal system are branches of which of the following vessels?
questions.why: The three embryonic gut divisions have distinct axial arteries. The coeliac trunk supplies abdominal foregut, the superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk supplies the abdominal foregut. Midgut and hindgut also contribute substantial parts of the abdominal gastrointestinal tract.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, including much of the small intestine and proximal colon. Foregut and hindgut have separate main arterial trunks.
notes.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut, including distal colon. It covers only one of the three embryonic territories.
notes.E: The three listed vascular trunks collectively supply the main foregut, midgut and hindgut territories within the abdomen.

questions.stem: The peritoneal cavity forms from which of the following?
questions.why: Spaces within the lateral plate mesoderm unite to form the intraembryonic coelom. Its abdominal portion becomes the peritoneal cavity as the body cavities are partitioned.

notes.A: The extraembryonic coelom forms the chorionic cavity outside the embryo. It is distinct from the developing internal body cavities.
notes.C: Somatic mesoderm contributes to the parietal peritoneal lining. The cavity itself comes from the space between lateral plate layers.
notes.D: The yolk sac contributes endoderm to the developing gut tube. The peritoneal cavity lies outside the tube.
notes.E: The blastocyst cavity forms before implantation. The definitive peritoneal cavity develops later within lateral plate mesoderm.

questions.stem: The following peritoneal ligaments are derived wholly or in part from the embryonic dorsal mesogastrium, EXCEPT:
questions.why: The liver divides the ventral mesogastrium into the falciform ligament and lesser omentum. The hepatogastric ligament is the portion of the lesser omentum between liver and stomach.

notes.B: The splenorenal ligament is the dorsal mesogastric fold between the spleen and posterior abdominal wall near the left kidney.
notes.C: The gastrosplenic ligament is a dorsal mesogastric connection between the greater curvature of the stomach and the spleen.
notes.D: The dorsal mesogastrium expands into the greater omentum, including its part between the stomach and transverse colon.
notes.E: The transverse mesocolon begins as colonic dorsal mesentery and later fuses with the greater omentum derived from dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.stem: Tracheoesophageal fistula results from:

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormal epithelial proliferation causing luminal obliteration

questions.why: The embryonic foregut normally separates into a ventral respiratory tract and a dorsal oesophagus. Abnormal partitioning can leave a persistent opening between the two lumens.

notes.A: Abnormal septum development does explain a fistula. The ridge-fusion description is the corresponding classical account of septum formation.
notes.B: Improper ridge fusion is one classical description of defective foregut partitioning. The corresponding septal abnormality is also listed.
notes.C: Incomplete reopening of the oesophageal lumen can cause a web or narrowing. A fistula requires an abnormal connection to the respiratory tract.
notes.D: Excess epithelial growth can narrow or occlude a lumen. It does not by itself establish a separate opening into the trachea.

questions.stem: The derivatives of the (embryonic) ventral mesentery include ALL the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The ventral mesentery gives rise to the falciform ligament, lesser omentum and coronary ligaments; the splenorenal ligament is a derivative of the DORSAL mesentery, so it is the exception.

notes.A: Ventral.
notes.B: Ventral.
notes.D: Ventral.
notes.E: Ventral.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the midgut include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The embryonic midgut forms bowel from the distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The descending colon lies in the hindgut territory.

notes.A: The duodenum below the major papilla is midgut-derived and receives superior mesenteric branches through pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
notes.B: The jejunum is formed from the midgut loop. Its branches arise from the superior mesenteric arterial system.
notes.C: The ileum is a midgut derivative and develops in continuity with bowel adjoining the embryonic vitelline duct.
notes.D: The ascending colon develops from the caudal limb of the midgut loop and remains in the superior mesenteric territory.

questions.stem: Arterial supply of structures derived from the hindgut is provided by which of the following?
questions.why: The inferior mesenteric artery is the main axial vessel of the embryonic hindgut. Its left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal branches serve corresponding derivatives in the adult.

notes.A: The coeliac trunk principally supplies foregut derivatives such as the stomach and proximal duodenum.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut derivatives from distal duodenum through proximal transverse colon.
notes.D: Internal iliac branches can supply the lower rectum and pelvic structures. The inferior mesenteric artery is the main hindgut artery.
notes.E: The external iliac artery primarily continues into the lower limb as the femoral artery. It is not a gut axial vessel.

questions.stem: During embryonic folding/movement, which of the following anomalies results when there is failure of closure of the lateral body wall leading to exposure of abdominal contents?
questions.why: Gastroschisis exposes abdominal viscera through a full-thickness paraumbilical wall defect without a covering sac. Failed lateral body wall closure is one classical explanation for this morphology.

notes.A: Omphalocoele is centred at the umbilical ring and herniated viscera are ordinarily covered by a sac.
notes.C: Meckel’s diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct at the ileum. It is not an exposed abdominal wall defect.
notes.D: An umbilical hernia protrudes through the umbilical ring beneath the skin. A bare lateral defect is a different finding.
notes.E: Only gastroschisis matches exposed bowel through a lateral wall defect. The other conditions have different anatomy or coverings.

questions.stem: About development of the alimentary canal:

options.label: A
options.text: The caudal limit of the pharyngeal gut is the tracheobronchial diverticulum

options.label: B
options.text: The foregut lies within the cephalic flexure, ventral to the heart tube

options.label: C
options.text: The hindgut ends at the cloacal membrane

options.label: D
options.text: The parenchyma of the accessory glands comes from endoderm

options.label: E
options.text: The muscle and peritoneal coats come from SOMATIC mesoderm

notes.A: The respiratory diverticulum marks the caudal level of the pharyngeal segment, where the ventral respiratory primordium forms.
notes.B: The foregut lies dorsal to the developing heart in the folded embryo. The heart tube is ventral to it.
notes.C: The early hindgut ends at the cloacal membrane, the temporary caudal boundary of the cloacal region.
notes.D: Gut-derived accessory glands such as the liver and pancreas have endodermal epithelial parenchyma and mesodermal supporting stroma.
notes.E: Splanchnic mesoderm provides gut smooth muscle and visceral serosa. Somatic mesoderm contributes to the parietal peritoneum.

questions.why: The primitive gut extends between the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes. Gut endoderm forms the lining and many glandular cells, while splanchnic mesoderm provides smooth muscle and visceral coverings.

questions.stem: Structures derived from the ventral mesogastrium include the:

notes.A: The falciform ligament connects the developing liver to the anterior abdominal wall and carries the umbilical vein in its free edge.
notes.B: Peritoneal reflections from the liver to the diaphragm form the coronary ligaments around the bare area.
notes.C: The hepatoduodenal ligament is the thickened free edge of the lesser omentum, between the liver and proximal duodenum.
notes.D: The lesser omentum is the ventral fold from liver to stomach and proximal duodenum.
notes.E: The greater omentum extends from the greater gastric curvature and develops from elongation of the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.why: Growth of the liver partitions the ventral mesogastrium into peritoneal folds around the liver and foregut. The greater omentum instead develops from the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.stem: About development of the pancreas:

options.label: A
options.text: The duodenal end of the dorsal bud duct may persist as the accessory pancreatic duct

options.label: B
options.text: The main pancreatic duct is formed by the ventral duct and the distal dorsal duct

options.label: C
options.text: The uncinate process develops entirely from the dorsal bud

options.label: D
options.text: The body and tail come wholly from the dorsal bud

options.label: E
options.text: The neck comes from the ventral bud

notes.A: The segment leading to the original dorsal opening can remain patent as the accessory duct at the minor papilla.
notes.B: The ventral duct forms the outlet segment of the main duct. The joined dorsal duct drains the body and tail.
notes.C: The uncinate process is a ventral bud derivative that passes behind the superior mesenteric vessels as the pancreas develops.
notes.D: The body and tail extend from the dorsal bud to form the elongated portion of the mature gland.
notes.E: The neck is chiefly dorsal in origin. The principal ventral derivatives are the uncinate process and inferior head.

questions.why: The ventral pancreatic bud forms part of the head and uncinate process. The dorsal bud forms most of the gland, and the two duct systems usually unite.

questions.stem: Which of the following mesodermal tissues directly gives rise to nephrons in the urinary system?
questions.why: The metanephric mesenchyme develops within intermediate mesoderm and gives rise to nephrons. The adjacent ureteric bud induces these nephrons and separately forms their collecting system.

notes.A: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and their derivatives. The nephrogenic cord forms lateral to the somites in intermediate mesoderm.
notes.B: Splanchnic mesoderm forms gut smooth muscle and visceral coverings. Renal nephrons arise from the metanephric mesenchyme.
notes.C: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall structures and parietal serosa. It does not form the nephrogenic cord.
notes.D: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures such as chorion and connecting stalk. The nephron progenitors lie inside the embryo.

questions.stem: The ureteric bud that becomes the ureter arises as an outgrowth from which of the following?
questions.why: The ureteric bud sprouts from the caudal mesonephric duct before it enters the cloaca. Its stalk forms the ureter and its branching tip forms collecting structures.

notes.A: The allantois connects to the developing bladder apex and contributes to the urachus. The ureteric bud sprouts more dorsally.
notes.C: The cloaca receives the mesonephric ducts. The bud emerges from a duct close to its cloacal entry.
notes.D: The common nephric duct is the segment caudal to the budding point. Its remodelling helps separate the ureteral and mesonephric openings.
notes.E: The primitive bladder receives the rearranged ureteral orifices later. The buds first grow from the paired mesonephric ducts.

questions.stem: What is the explanation for congenital polycystic kidney?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of the ureteric bud to form an ampulla

options.label: B
options.text: Divisions of the ureteric ampulla that to occur synchronously

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of formation of nephrons from metanephric caps

options.label: D
options.text: Large numbers of nephrons that fail to unite with ureteric bud ampulla

options.label: E
options.text: Ureteric bud divisions that occur asynchronously but not asymmetrically

questions.why: The classic explanation is nephrons that fail to join collecting tubules, so they swell into cysts.

notes.A: Would give renal agenesis.
notes.B: Not a cause.
notes.C: Would give a hypoplastic kidney.
notes.E: Not a cause.

questions.stem: Which of the structures below is absorbed into the wall of the urinary bladder in the course of development?
questions.why: The common nephric duct is the short caudal mesonephric segment shared by the ureter and genital duct before their openings separate. Its remodelling helps position the ureter in the bladder wall.

notes.A: The paramesonephric duct contributes to female reproductive structures. It is distinct from the common segment linking the urinary ducts to the sinus.
notes.B: The ureteric bud forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. Its opening is repositioned during bladder development.
notes.C: The allantois connects at the bladder apex and becomes the urachus. The common duct remodels in the posterior bladder region.
notes.D: The vesical urogenital sinus gives rise to the developing bladder. Its wall receives the opening of the nephric duct system.

questions.stem: A 70-year old man comes to your clinic with a watery discharge from his umbilicus. On questioning you find that he has a confirmed enlarged prostate with urethral obstruction. What is the explanation for his umbilical discharge?

options.label: A
options.text: Mucus dicaharge from a sinus of vitelline duct

options.label: B
options.text: Mucus discharge from and umbilical fistula

options.label: C
options.text: Urine discharge through a patent urachus

options.label: E
options.text: Weeping gastric ulcer in a Meckel’s diverticulum

questions.why: A patent urachus retains a continuous channel from the bladder apex to the umbilicus. Raised bladder pressure from outlet obstruction can make urine discharge through it.

notes.A: A vitelline sinus is an umbilical remnant of the intestinal duct. Its secretion has no direct relationship to bladder outlet pressure.
notes.B: Mucus discharge can arise from an intestinal remnant. The combination of watery discharge and outlet obstruction favours a bladder connection.
notes.D: An umbilical hernia contains tissue protruding through the ring. Routine herniation does not create a channel from the bladder.
notes.E: Meckel’s diverticulum is usually blind-ending within the abdomen. Ulceration classically causes intestinal bleeding rather than urinary discharge.

questions.stem: The kidney and ureter develop from which of the following?
questions.why: Both major components of the definitive kidney arise in intermediate mesoderm. The metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons and the ureteric bud forms the ureter and collecting system.

notes.B: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall and visceral tissues. The nephrogenic cord is in intermediate mesoderm.
notes.C: Paraxial mesoderm produces somites, which contribute to vertebrae and skeletal muscle. The renal primordia arise lateral to them.
notes.D: Endoderm contributes much of the bladder epithelium through the urogenital sinus. The upper urinary tract is mesodermal.
notes.E: Ectoderm forms structures including epidermis and nervous tissue. Nephrons and ureters develop from the nephrogenic region of mesoderm.

questions.stem: During development, rotation of the kidney occurs around which axis?
questions.why: As the kidneys ascend from the pelvis, each rotates medially around its longitudinal axis. This turns the hilum from an anterior orientation towards the midline.

notes.B: Rotation about a transverse axis would tilt the upper and lower poles. The typical change is medial orientation of the hilum.
notes.C: A sagittal axis runs from front to back. The kidney’s developmental rotation is around the line between its poles.
notes.D: The developing kidney turns around its own long axis, defined by the superior and inferior poles.
notes.E: An anteroposterior axis is horizontal in the anatomical position. The renal poles mark a roughly longitudinal axis.

questions.stem: All of the following anomalies of kidney development may occur EXCEPT:
questions.why: Abnormal renal development can affect formation, fusion, ascent or tubule architecture. An accessory spleen instead reflects separate development of splenic tissue in the dorsal mesogastrium.

notes.A: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion, usually of the lower poles. The fused renal mass may have restricted ascent.
notes.B: A pelvic kidney remains low because the normal ascent of the metanephric kidney is incomplete.
notes.C: Renal agenesis results when a kidney fails to form, often because induction of metanephric tissue is disrupted.
notes.D: Polycystic kidney disease can present congenitally. Abnormal cyst formation occurs in renal tubular or collecting duct epithelium.

questions.stem: The trigone of the urinary bladder is formed by absorption of which structure?
questions.why: The caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts are absorbed to form the trigone.

notes.B: Opens into it.
notes.C: Female ducts.
notes.D: Divided first.
notes.E: Urachus.

questions.stem: What explains the lobulated surface of fetal kidneys?
questions.why: Developing renal lobes remain outlined by grooves at the fetal kidney surface. As surrounding cortical tissue grows after birth, the grooves often become less conspicuous.

notes.A: Distinct surface grooves are visible between lobes before the cortex smooths their outlines. Complete fusion would reduce visible lobulation.
notes.C: Cortical growth is associated with smoothing of the surface after birth. The fetal pattern reflects still-visible boundaries between lobes.
notes.D: Each lobe contains a medullary pyramid and related cortex. Normal fetal lobulation does not require degeneration of the medulla.
notes.E: Normal ureteric branching helps establish lobar territories. Visible fetal lobulation does not imply a branching anomaly.

questions.stem: Which of the following system of kidney develops from the cranial portion of the nephric ridge?
questions.why: The pronephros is the first, rudimentary nephric system and appears at the cranial end of the nephrogenic ridge. It regresses without serving as a functioning human kidney.

notes.A: The metanephros develops caudally in the pelvis and forms the permanent kidney following interaction with the ureteric bud.
notes.C: The temporary mesonephros forms caudal to the pronephros and develops more functional tubules during early embryonic life.
notes.D: The paramesonephric duct forms beside the mesonephros and contributes to reproductive structures rather than a cranial kidney system.
notes.E: The ureteric bud sprouts from the caudal mesonephric duct and induces the metanephros. It arises much farther caudally.

questions.stem: Which of the following has a dual origin of development?
questions.why: Trigone: mesoderm (mesonephric ducts) and endoderm (sinus). Kidney: ureteric bud and metanephric blastema.

notes.A: Both.
notes.B: Both.
notes.C: Single.
notes.E: Some do.

questions.stem: Which of the following anomalies of kidney development results from fusion?
questions.why: A horseshoe kidney usually forms when the lower poles of the two metanephric kidneys fuse. The connecting isthmus can limit their normal ascent into the abdomen.

notes.A: Unilateral agenesis means one kidney fails to form. It does not involve joining two renal poles.
notes.B: In bilateral agenesis, neither kidney develops. Fusion requires two developing renal masses.
notes.D: A pelvic kidney typically reflects failure of ascent. Fusion can restrict ascent but is not required for pelvic ectopia.
notes.E: Multicystic dysplastic kidney reflects abnormal renal differentiation with cysts and disorganised tissue. It is not defined by fusion.

questions.stem: From which of the following does the urinary bladder develop?

options.label: B
options.text: Upper part of primitive urogenital sinus

options.label: C
options.text: Upper part of umbilical urogenital sinus

questions.why: The upper vesical portion of the primitive urogenital sinus expands to form most of the urinary bladder. Its apex is temporarily continuous with the allantois.

notes.A: The cloaca is the earlier common chamber. Its ventral urogenital subdivision supplies the immediate bladder primordium.
notes.C: The allantoic connection extends toward the umbilicus. The named bladder-forming region is the vesical part of the primitive urogenital sinus.
notes.D: The common nephric duct remodels near the posterior bladder and helps separate the duct openings. It does not produce most of the bladder.
notes.E: The ureteric bud forms the upper collecting tract. The bladder expands from the urogenital sinus.

questions.stem: RU486 (mifepristone) directly antagonizes:

notes.A: Human chorionic gonadotrophin signals through the LH receptor to support early luteal function. It is not the direct target here.
notes.B: Human placental lactogen acts through lactogenic and related pathways. Mifepristone acts primarily at steroid receptors.
notes.C: Relaxin uses its own receptor and contributes to connective tissue and vascular changes. The drug does not directly block relaxin signalling.
notes.D: Mifepristone competes at progesterone receptors and blocks transcriptional responses that depend on progesterone.
notes.E: Oestrogen signals through distinct nuclear receptors. Mifepristone’s relevant direct target here is the progesterone receptor.

questions.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptor signalling. In pregnancy, this interferes with progesterone-dependent support of the decidua and increases uterine responsiveness to prostaglandins.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the mesonephric duct in the male genital system includes ALL of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The male mesonephric duct persists as much of the sperm-conducting tract. Seminiferous tubules instead develop from the testis cords within the gonadal primordium.

notes.A: The terminal mesonephric duct beyond the seminal vesicle outgrowth forms the ejaculatory duct.
notes.B: Each seminal vesicle forms as an outgrowth of the distal mesonephric duct and provides secretions to the genital tract.
notes.C: The duct of the epididymis develops from a coiled portion of the mesonephric duct. The efferent ductules come from mesonephric tubules.
notes.D: The mesonephric duct elongates into the ductus deferens, which carries sperm from the epididymis towards the ejaculatory duct.

questions.stem: Which cells produce Mullerian Inhibiting hormone (MIH) that is responsible for the degeneration of the paramesonephric ducts in a male foetus?
questions.why: Differentiating Sertoli cells in the fetal testis secrete anti-Müllerian hormone. Its signalling induces regression of the Müllerian ducts, while androgen signalling supports separate male duct development.

notes.A: Primordial germ cells migrate to the genital ridge and form the germ line. Anti-Müllerian hormone comes from somatic Sertoli cells.
notes.C: Spermatogonia are germ-line cells in the testis cords and are precursors of sperm. They are not the source of the hormone.
notes.D: Testis cords contain developing Sertoli cells and germ cells. Sertoli cells are the specific secreting population within the cords.
notes.E: Surrounding mesenchyme participates in the duct’s response to the hormone. The fetal Sertoli cells provide the signal.

questions.stem: Which cells directly form spermatogonia in a differentiating gonadal/genital ridge?
questions.why: Primordial germ cells migrate to the developing gonadal ridges. In a differentiating testis their descendants enter the germ cell lineage that gives rise to spermatogonia.

notes.A: Gonadal mesenchyme contributes supporting stroma and interstitial cells. Spermatogonia belong to the separate germ-cell lineage.
notes.B: Somatic testis cord cells include supporting Sertoli cells. The germ cells within the cords descend from migrating primordial germ cells.
notes.D: The mesonephric duct contributes to parts of the genital drainage tract. Its epithelial cells do not become spermatogonia.
notes.E: Coelomic epithelium forms part of the gonadal primordium. Germ-line precursors arrive by migration.

questions.stem: The clitoris develops from which of the following?
questions.why: The genital tubercle is the common early phallic primordium. In typical female development it gives rise to the clitoris, homologous to the male penis.

notes.A: The urogenital folds remain separate in typical female development and form the labia minora beside the vestibule.
notes.C: The mesonephric duct largely regresses in typical female development. It is not part of the external phallic primordium.
notes.D: Paramesonephric ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and part of the vagina. The clitoris is external and tubercular in origin.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a temporary embryonic renal system. It does not give rise to the clitoris.

questions.stem: Which of the structures below is formed by fusion of paramesonephric ducts?
questions.why: The caudal paramesonephric ducts fuse to form the uterovaginal primordium, which gives rise to the uterus and cervix. The cranial portions remain separate as the uterine tubes.

notes.B: The oviducts are uterine tubes. They form from the cranial portions of the paramesonephric ducts that remain separate.
notes.C: The ovary develops within the gonadal ridge, where primordial germ cells join the supporting somatic cells.
notes.D: The labia minora form from the paired urogenital folds beside the developing vestibule.
notes.E: The labioscrotal swellings form the labia majora. They develop externally and are separate from the fused internal ducts.

questions.stem: Which of the underlisted structures forms the ovary?
questions.why: The ovary differentiates in the gonadal ridge after primordial germ cells arrive. These germ cells and somatic populations in the ridge participate in follicle formation.

notes.A: Genital swellings in the external primordia form the labia majora. The ovary develops internally in the gonadal ridge.
notes.B: The genital tubercle forms the clitoris in female development. It is part of the external genital primordium.
notes.C: The paired genital folds form the labia minora. They are external structures flanking the vestibule.
notes.E: The mesonephros is the transient embryonic renal system adjacent to the gonad. The ovarian primordium is the gonadal ridge.

questions.stem: The vaginal plate that canalizes to form the vagina develops from proliferation of which of the following?
questions.why: In the classical description, paired sinovaginal bulbs proliferate from the urogenital sinus where it meets the uterovaginal primordium. They form a solid vaginal plate that later canalises.

notes.B: The urogenital membrane forms a temporary covering over the early outlet and later ruptures. The epithelial proliferations arise from the sinus wall.
notes.C: The fused paramesonephric ducts form the uterovaginal primordium and contact the sinus. The sinovaginal bulbs are outgrowths at this junction.
notes.D: The genital tubercle gives rise to the clitoris in female development. The vaginal plate develops internally at the sinus.
notes.E: Genital folds flank the vestibule and give rise to the labia minora. They do not form the vaginal plate.

questions.stem: In the development of the ovary, which primordial cells form the follicular cells?
questions.why: Cortical sex cords (from coelomic epithelium) surround the oogonia as follicular cells.

notes.B: Stroma.
notes.C: They first give the sex cords.
notes.D: Become oogonia.
notes.E: One is correct.

questions.stem: The oviducts develop from which of the embryonic structures below?
questions.why: The unfused cranial paramesonephric ducts give rise to the two uterine tubes. Their caudal portions instead unite to form the midline uterovaginal primordium.

notes.A: The genital folds remain separate as the labia minora. They are part of the external genital primordium.
notes.B: The genital ridge supplies the gonadal primordium. The uterine tubes form from the neighbouring paramesonephric ducts.
notes.C: The genital tubercle forms the clitoris in female development. The uterine tubes are internal duct derivatives.
notes.D: The mesonephric ducts largely regress in female development and may leave remnants, including Gartner duct tissue.

questions.stem: The testis develops from which of the following structures in the embryo?
questions.why: The testis differentiates within the gonadal ridge. In typical 46,XY development, SRY-driven signalling promotes Sertoli cell differentiation and the organisation of testis cords.

notes.B: The mesonephros lies next to the gonad. Some mesonephric tubules form efferent ductules rather than the gonad itself.
notes.C: The genital tubercle forms the principal phallic primordium. It is separate from the developing testis.
notes.D: The genital folds contribute to the ventral penis and enclose much of the spongy urethra. They are external primordia.
notes.E: The labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum. The testis develops initially much higher at the gonadal ridge.

questions.stem: The penis develops mainly from which embryonic structure?
questions.why: The genital tubercle elongates to form the phallus under androgen signalling. In typical male development this forms most of the penis, with contributions from adjacent folds.

notes.B: The gonadal ridge differentiates into a testis. Hormones from the gonad influence development of the separate external genital primordia.
notes.C: The urethral folds join along the underside of the phallus, enclosing much of the urethra. The main phallic mass comes from the tubercle.
notes.D: The labioscrotal swellings fuse to form the scrotum. They do not form the main shaft of the phallus.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a transient renal structure. Its derivatives in the male tract do not form the external phallus.

questions.stem: The following statements are correct concerning the descent of the testis

options.label: A
options.text: Testosterone is required for successful descent

options.label: B
options.text: There is no descent without the gubernaculum testis

options.label: C
options.text: Descent is necessary for the proper formation of the inguinal canal

options.label: D
options.text: The processus vaginalis completely encloses the testis on all sides during descent

options.label: E
options.text: The internal spermatic fascia develops from the internal oblique muscle

options.label: F
options.text: The cremasteric fascia develops from the fascia transversalis

options.label: G
options.text: The external spermatic fascia develops from the external oblique aponeurosis

options.label: H
options.text: A persistent communication of the processus vaginalis with the peritoneal cavity gives rise to a congenital inguinal hernia

notes.A: Androgen signalling is important in the later inguinoscrotal phase. INSL3 has a major role in the earlier transabdominal phase.
notes.B: The gubernaculum anchors and guides the testis during development. Abnormal gubernacular development can contribute to failed descent.
notes.C: The inguinal region develops before the testis traverses it. Descent uses and modifies a developing passage rather than initiating it.
notes.D: The distal processus vaginalis becomes the tunica vaginalis, which covers anterior and lateral surfaces without enclosing the posterior attachment.
notes.E: The internal spermatic fascia comes from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring as the testis passes through.
notes.F: The cremasteric fascia and muscle are derived chiefly from the internal oblique layer rather than the transversalis fascia.
notes.G: The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis near the superficial inguinal ring.
notes.H: A patent processus vaginalis can transmit abdominal contents into the inguinal canal, producing an indirect hernia.

questions.why: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent, with androgen signalling especially important during the inguinoscrotal phase. The processus vaginalis normally loses its connection to the peritoneal cavity.

questions.stem: An XY fetus that develops female external genitalia will have:

options.label: F
options.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome as the likely cause

notes.A: The testes still make AMH, so the paramesonephric ducts regress and no oviducts form.
notes.B: SRY on the Y chromosome makes the gonads testes, not ovaries.
notes.C: SRY directs the gonads to become testes, even though the body cannot respond to their androgens.
notes.D: Without androgen action the mesonephric ducts regress, so there is no ductus deferens.
notes.E: The epididymis is also a mesonephric (Wolffian) derivative and needs androgen action to persist.
notes.F: A defective androgen receptor in an XY individual gives female external genitalia despite testes.
notes.G: The testes usually remain undescended, in the abdomen or inguinal canal.
notes.H: With no uterus or tubes and non-functional testes, the person cannot reproduce.
notes.I: AMH from the testes makes the paramesonephric ducts regress, so no uterus forms.

questions.why: In androgen insensitivity the XY testes make AMH (so no Müllerian structures) and testosterone, but the tissues cannot respond, so the Wolffian ducts regress and the external genitalia develop as female.

questions.stem: Which structure in the testis prevents autoimmune destruction of developing sperm?

options.label: B
options.text: Basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium

questions.why: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells separate the basal and adluminal compartments of seminiferous tubules. This limits exposure of developing germ cell antigens to the systemic immune environment.

notes.B: The basement membrane supports the seminiferous epithelium. The main barrier between basal and adluminal germ-cell compartments is junctional.
notes.C: Leydig cells lie in the interstitium and release testosterone. They are outside the Sertoli cell junctional barrier.
notes.D: Sertoli cell processes support and enclose developing germ cells locally. Tight junctions between neighbouring Sertoli cells provide the seal.
notes.E: Peritubular myoid cells surround the tubules and aid peristaltic movement. They do not separate basal from adluminal cells.

questions.stem: Which cell in the testis produces testosterone?
questions.why: Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium produce testosterone. Luteinising hormone stimulates their steroid synthesis, supporting spermatogenesis and androgen-dependent development.

notes.B: Sertoli cells support germ cells and respond to follicle-stimulating hormone. They are not the principal source of testosterone.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes are germ cells undergoing meiosis. Testosterone is synthesised in adjacent interstitial Leydig cells.
notes.D: Myoid cells lie around seminiferous tubules and help propel luminal fluid. Their main role here is contractile.
