notes.E: Spermatids are haploid germ cells that remodel into spermatozoa. They do not provide testicular androgen secretion.

questions.stem: Which cell forms the blood–testis barrier?
questions.why: Adjacent Sertoli cells form tight junctions near the base of seminiferous tubules. These junctions create the blood–testis barrier and maintain a distinct environment for germ cells.

notes.B: Leydig cells are outside the tubules and produce testosterone. They do not form the epithelial junctional seal.
notes.C: Myoid cells form a contractile layer outside seminiferous epithelium. The barrier within the tubule is formed by Sertoli cells.
notes.D: Spermatogonia occupy the basal compartment and divide to supply germ cells. The junctional seal lies between supporting Sertoli cells.
notes.E: Fibroblasts produce extracellular matrix in supporting tissues. They do not form the tight junctions that divide the seminiferous epithelium.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates testosterone secretion at puberty?
questions.why: Pituitary luteinising hormone stimulates interstitial Leydig cells to produce testosterone at puberty. Its older name, interstitial cell-stimulating hormone, refers to that direct testicular action.

notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts primarily on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis. Leydig cell steroid production is stimulated directly by luteinising hormone.
notes.C: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone stimulates the pituitary to release gonadotrophins. It acts upstream of the direct Leydig cell signal.
notes.D: Inhibin from Sertoli cells provides negative feedback on pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone release. It does not stimulate Leydig cells.
notes.E: Prolactin is associated primarily with lactation and does not supply the main direct pubertal stimulus for testosterone production.

questions.stem: The main type of follicle in the ovary before puberty is the:
questions.why: The prepubertal ovarian reserve consists predominantly of primordial follicles. Each contains a primary oocyte arrested in meiotic prophase and surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular cells.

notes.B: A unilaminar primary follicle has one layer of cuboidal follicular cells. This is an activated stage beyond the resting reserve.
notes.C: Multiple granulosa cell layers develop in growing primary follicles. They represent a smaller subset than the primordial pool.
notes.D: Antral follicles have a fluid-filled cavity and are more advanced. They do not make up most of the prepubertal reserve.
notes.E: A Graafian follicle is a large preovulatory follicle. Prepubertal ovaries contain mostly resting primordial follicles.

questions.stem: The continual degeneration of follicles from fetal life through reproductive life is:
questions.why: Follicular atresia is degeneration of ovarian follicles that do not complete development. It occurs before birth and continues throughout reproductive life, gradually reducing the follicle reserve.

notes.B: Ovulation releases an oocyte from a selected mature follicle. It does not describe degeneration within the ovary.
notes.C: Luteinisation converts cells of an ovulated follicle into steroid-producing cells of the corpus luteum.
notes.D: Folliculogenesis refers to activation and growth of follicles. Atresia can interrupt that process at several stages.
notes.E: Menstruation is the shedding of uterine endometrium. It is separate from degeneration of ovarian follicles.

questions.stem: In sexual development, which is primarily established at fertilization?
questions.why: Fertilisation establishes the embryo’s chromosomal complement, including its sex chromosomes. Gonadal differentiation, hormone production and differentiation of ducts and external genitalia occur subsequently.

notes.A: External genitalia begin as common primordia. They differentiate later in response to local developmental and hormonal signalling.
notes.C: Both major duct systems are present in early embryos. Their subsequent development depends in part on gonadal hormone signals.
notes.D: The gonadal primordium initially has the potential to differentiate along different pathways, which become apparent weeks later.
notes.E: The developing gonads begin hormone production after they differentiate. These hormonal signals are downstream of the chromosomal complement.

questions.stem: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS), why are undescended testes removed?
questions.why: When gonadectomy is chosen in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, its purpose is to reduce future testicular tumour risk. Risk varies with age, so timing is individualised.

notes.A: Undescended testes experience a warmer environment, but gonadectomy in this condition is considered principally for tumour risk reduction.
notes.B: Androgen receptor dysfunction explains the phenotype. Removing the gonads does not restore androgen receptor function.
notes.C: Torsion is possible for an undescended gonad, but it is not the usual rationale for elective removal in this syndrome.
notes.D: Removal does not improve fertility. The clinical consideration in this stem is long-term gonadal tumour risk.

questions.stem: Formation of the uterus depends directly on which structure?
questions.why: The caudal Müllerian ducts fuse to form the uterovaginal primordium and generate the uterus and cervix. Failure of their formation or fusion can alter uterine development.

notes.B: The Wolffian ducts are mesonephric ducts. They form male internal genital duct structures when maintained by androgen signalling.
notes.C: The urogenital sinus contributes to the lower reproductive and urinary tract. The uterine primordium arises from the paired Müllerian ducts.
notes.D: Mesonephric ducts usually regress substantially in female development, whereas the paramesonephric ducts form the uterus.
notes.E: The urorectal septum separates developing anorectal and urogenital regions. It does not form the uterine wall.

questions.stem: Pure gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer syndrome) is caused by:
questions.why: A pathogenic SRY variant can prevent testis differentiation in a 46,XY embryo, producing complete gonadal dysgenesis. Other changes affecting the testis-determining pathway can produce the same phenotype.

notes.A: A Y chromosome is present in 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. A defect in the developmental pathway can occur despite that chromosome.
notes.C: Müllerian structures can persist because dysgenetic gonads produce little anti-Müllerian hormone. Their persistence is a consequence.
notes.D: The genital tubercle forms external genital structures. Its development does not determine whether the gonadal ridge differentiates as a testis.
notes.E: Mesonephric ducts can regress when gonadal androgen production is insufficient. Their loss does not initiate failure of gonadal differentiation.

questions.stem: Imperforate hymen results from:

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of the paramesonephric ducts to fuse

questions.why: An imperforate hymen results when the hymenal membrane fails to open at the vaginal outlet. The canal above it can otherwise develop normally.

notes.B: Failure of Müllerian duct fusion can cause uterine duplication or a longitudinal vaginal septum, rather than an unperforated hymenal membrane.
notes.C: Abnormal fusion between developmental components can cause deeper partitions. An imperforate hymen is at the vaginal outlet.
notes.D: Cloacal malformations affect separation of the anorectal and urogenital tracts. An isolated imperforate hymen involves the outlet membrane.
notes.E: A persistent urogenital sinus can produce a shared lower tract opening. The specific defect here is failure of hymenal opening.

questions.stem: Which hormone is responsible for development of the penis from the genital tubercle?
questions.why: Dihydrotestosterone is formed from testosterone by 5-alpha reductase in target tissues. Its androgen receptor signalling promotes male differentiation of the genital tubercle and adjacent external folds.

notes.A: Oestrogen has roles in reproductive development but does not supply the principal androgen signal for penile differentiation.
notes.B: Anti-Müllerian hormone induces regression of the Müllerian ducts. It does not directly masculinise the genital tubercle.
notes.C: Testosterone supplies the substrate for dihydrotestosterone and directly maintains Wolffian ducts. Conversion produces the main external genital signal.
notes.D: Progesterone acts through its own receptor. It does not provide the main masculinising signal to the phallic primordium.

questions.stem: Why is a longitudinal vaginal septum confined to the upper one-third of the vagina?

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion of Müllerian ducts forms upper vagina

options.label: B
options.text: Lower vagina develops from urogenital sinus

options.label: C
options.text: Upper vagina forms from mesonephric ducts

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of canalization of vaginal plate

questions.why: A longitudinal vaginal septum is confined to the upper third because that part forms by fusion of the paired Mullerian ducts, whereas the lower vagina derives from the single urogenital sinus.

notes.B: True but does not explain.
notes.C: No.
notes.D: Lower.
notes.E: No.

questions.stem: The prostate develops from which of the following embryonic structures?
questions.why: Prostatic glands develop as epithelial buds from the prostatic urethra, a derivative of the urogenital sinus. Surrounding mesenchyme provides the gland’s stromal and smooth muscle components.

notes.A: The cloaca is an earlier common chamber that gives rise to the urogenital sinus after partitioning. The sinus is the immediate source.
notes.C: The genital ridge forms the gonad. Prostatic gland buds instead grow from the adjacent urethral epithelium.
notes.D: The labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum in male development. They are external and do not form prostatic glands.
notes.E: The mesonephros is a transient kidney system. Prostatic epithelium arises from the urogenital sinus rather than from mesonephric tubules.

questions.stem: The gubernaculum in the female forms the:
questions.why: The uterus interrupts the female gubernaculum. Its segment from ovary to uterus forms the ovarian ligament, and the continuation toward the inguinal canal forms the uterine round ligament.

notes.A: The proper ovarian ligament is the segment of the gubernaculum between ovary and uterus. Its uterine continuation is also a derivative.
notes.B: The inguinal ligament is the rolled inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis. It is separate from the gubernaculum.
notes.C: The uterine round ligament is the segment continuing toward the inguinal canal. The segment above its uterine attachment also persists.
notes.D: The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum supporting the uterus and associated structures, with a different developmental origin.

questions.stem: A woman with double vagina may also have which of the following genital abnormalities?
questions.why: Incomplete fusion of the paired Müllerian ducts can leave duplicated uterine and cervical structures and a longitudinal vaginal septum. Uterus didelphys is a recognised associated finding.

notes.B: Ovaries develop from the gonadal ridges, independently of Müllerian duct fusion. They can be present with uterine duplication.
notes.C: Imperforate hymen affects opening of the distal outlet membrane. It does not follow directly from duplication of the paired duct system.
notes.D: Hypospadias is abnormal positioning of the urethral opening, classically associated with incomplete male urethral development.
notes.E: Cloacal exstrophy involves a broader abdominal wall and pelvic developmental defect. It is not the characteristic association described here.

questions.stem: Male differentiation of the indifferent external genitalia is under the direct influence of:
questions.why: Local conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone provides the main androgen signal for typical male differentiation of external genital primordia, including the genital tubercle and urogenital folds.

notes.B: Oestrogen participates in other aspects of reproductive development. It is not the androgen receptor ligand directing external masculinisation.
notes.C: Anti-Müllerian hormone causes regression of internal Müllerian ducts, a separate process from differentiation of the external genitalia.
notes.D: Progesterone is important in reproductive physiology through progesterone receptors. The direct masculinising signal here acts through androgen receptors.
notes.E: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal supporting cells. It is not the direct morphogenetic signal to the external genital primordia.

questions.stem: A young woman complained to her consultant that she noticed her baby is having swelling in the inguinal region, which is increasing in size. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.why: A persistent processus vaginalis leaves a channel between the peritoneal cavity and inguinal canal. Abdominal contents or fluid entering it can produce an enlarging groin swelling.

notes.A: Abnormal gubernacular development can impair testicular descent. An enlarging groin swelling fits a persistent channel that transmits fluid or viscera.
notes.C: An undescended testis can be palpable in the groin. A swelling that changes with herniation is more consistent with an open processus.
notes.D: Enlarged nodes can cause discrete groin lumps, but they do not provide a congenital channel from the abdominal cavity.
notes.E: In infants the typical indirect hernia follows the existing inguinal pathway through a patent processus rather than a primary muscle defect.

questions.stem: Bilateral undescended testes cause infertility mainly because of:

options.label: C
options.text: Inability to release sperms during ejaculation,

questions.why: Bilateral cryptorchidism puts both testes outside the cooler scrotal environment. Seminiferous epithelium and germ cells are particularly vulnerable, reducing sperm production and later fertility.

notes.B: Leydig endocrine function can be relatively preserved even when sperm production is impaired by the higher temperature.
notes.C: Ejaculation depends on separate ductal and neuromuscular pathways. In cryptorchidism the principal problem is production of mature sperm.
notes.D: Primary ciliary dyskinesia can impair sperm motility. It does not explain injury to the germinal epithelium of undescended testes.
notes.E: Dihydrotestosterone supports external genital development. Reduced spermatogenesis is the main mechanism asked for after bilateral non-descent.

questions.stem: What is the commonest cause of female infertility?
questions.why: Ovulatory dysfunction is a common cause of female infertility. Without regular release of an oocyte, opportunities for spontaneous fertilisation decrease, even when the tubes and uterus are normal.

notes.B: Bilateral tubal obstruction prevents sperm and oocyte meeting. It is an important cause, but ovulatory dysfunction is more common overall.
notes.C: Coital factors can reduce opportunities for fertilisation. The common reproductive mechanism listed here is disruption of oocyte release.
notes.D: Endometrial receptivity matters for implantation, but isolated timing of the endometrial cycle is not the leading established cause listed.
notes.E: Endometriosis can affect fertility through pelvic inflammation or altered anatomy. Ovulatory problems are reported more commonly overall.

questions.stem: Deficiency in the microtubules of spermatozoa is clinically called:
questions.why: Defective microtubule (dynein) arms leave sperm immotile.

notes.A: Few sperm.
notes.B: No sperm.
notes.C: Not microtubular.
notes.E: Urethral.

questions.stem: The blood-testis barrier is formed between which of the following when they are adjacent?

options.label: A
options.text: Type A and Type B spermatogonia

options.label: C
options.text: Sertoli cell and another Sertoli cell

options.label: D
options.text: Seminiferous tubule and another seminiferous tubule

questions.why: The blood–testis barrier forms at junctions between neighbouring Sertoli cells. Their seals separate basal spermatogonia from germ cells undergoing later stages of development in the adluminal compartment.

notes.A: Spermatogonia are germ cells in the basal compartment. The seal is formed by adjacent somatic supporting cells.
notes.B: Sertoli cells closely support spermatocytes, but the continuous junctional barrier lies between neighbouring Sertoli cells.
notes.D: Each tubule contains its own junctional barrier. A boundary between two tubules is outside the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.E: Leydig cells and peritubular myoid cells lie outside the seminiferous epithelium. The tight junctions are within that epithelium.

questions.stem: Which of the following are functions of the testis? i. Secretion of testosterone ii. Manufacture of male germ cells iii. Secretion of luteinising hormone iv. Secretion of follicle stimulating hormone v. Secretion of testicular fluid
questions.why: Leydig cells secrete testosterone, while the seminiferous epithelium produces the male germ cells and Sertoli cells contribute luminal fluid. The pituitary supplies the testis-regulating gonadotrophins.

notes.A: Androgen secretion and germ-cell production are both testicular functions. Sertoli cells also provide fluid within the seminiferous tubules.
notes.B: The testis does produce testosterone and male germ cells. Luteinising hormone is released by anterior pituitary gonadotrophs.
notes.C: Testicular fluid is produced locally, but both gonadotrophins originate in the anterior pituitary and act on the testis.
notes.E: The testis supplies germ cells and testicular fluid. Follicle-stimulating hormone comes from the anterior pituitary.

questions.stem: Derivatives of neural crest cells include:

notes.A: Migrating melanoblasts derived from the neural crest populate tissues such as skin and differentiate into melanocytes.
notes.B: Schwann cells develop from neural crest derivatives and form supporting and myelinating glia around peripheral axons.
notes.C: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells belong to the neural crest lineage and secrete catecholamines into the circulation.
notes.D: Embryonic dermatomes form from somites in paraxial mesoderm. They contribute to dermis rather than a neural crest lineage.
notes.E: Neural crest cells form the sensory neurons and supporting glia of the dorsal root ganglia.

questions.why: Neural crest cells migrate from the closing neural tube and generate multiple peripheral lineages, including sensory neurons, Schwann cells, pigment cells and adrenal chromaffin cells.

questions.stem: ALL of the following arise from neural crest cells, EXCEPT:
questions.why: Ependyma comes from the neuroepithelium of the neural tube.

notes.B: Neural crest.
notes.C: Neural crest.
notes.D: Neural crest.
notes.E: Neural crest (via ultimobranchial body).

questions.stem: During development of the nervous system, ALL of the following neuroglial cells derive from the neuroepithelium of the neural tube, EXCEPT:
questions.why: Microglia arise mainly from early yolk-sac macrophage precursors that colonise the developing central nervous system. Ependymal cells, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes instead derive from neural tube progenitors.

notes.B: Ependymal cells arise from neuroepithelial or radial glial progenitors and form the lining of the ventricles and spinal central canal.
notes.C: Astrocytes differentiate from central neuroectodermal progenitors and provide support within neural tissue.
notes.D: Oligodendrocytes arise from progenitors within the developing central nervous system and form central myelin.
notes.E: Microglia provide a clear exception because their normal developmental origin is the embryonic myeloid lineage.

questions.stem: In the developing neural tube, primitive neurocytes migrate to lie outside the external limiting membrane of the neuroepithelium where they form which of the following?
questions.why: Neuroblasts form the mantle layer (future grey matter).

notes.A: The inner neuroepithelial layer.
notes.B: Outer, axons (white matter).
notes.D: Lines the canal.
notes.E: Separate cells from the folds.

questions.stem: Congenital hydrocephalus may be caused by the following faults in the development of the brain

options.label: A
options.text: Blockage of the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)

options.label: B
options.text: Inadequate or failure of development of the interventricular foramen (of Monro)

options.label: C
options.text: Failure of the development of the foramen of Luschka and Magendie in the 4th ventricle

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of development of the choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles

notes.A: Aqueductal obstruction prevents fluid passing from the third to the fourth ventricle and enlarges the upstream ventricles.
notes.B: The interventricular foramina allow drainage from each lateral ventricle. Obstruction can cause enlargement of the affected lateral ventricle.
notes.C: The median and lateral fourth ventricular apertures allow fluid to reach the subarachnoid space. Their obstruction raises upstream volume.
notes.D: Choroid plexus contributes to fluid production. Its failure to develop is not a blockage at a ventricular outlet.

questions.why: Congenital obstruction at a ventricular connection can prevent normal cerebrospinal fluid drainage. Fluid accumulates upstream and enlarges the affected ventricles, producing obstructive hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: Whether or not the primary cause of spina bifida is complete or incomplete, as well as the extent of faulty development of related mesoderm results in several different clinical forms. The forms below have the stated presentation and/or features

options.label: A
options.text: In meningocoele, there is a cystic swelling beneath the skin that contains cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: B
options.text: In meningocoele, the spinal cord and nerves are abnormal

options.label: C
options.text: Myelocoele is characterized by an oval raw area found in the surface of the affected area

options.label: D
options.text: In myelocoele the spinal cord and nerves are normal

notes.A: Meninges protrude through the vertebral defect and enclose cerebrospinal fluid. A membrane or skin can cover the swelling.
notes.B: A simple meningocoele contains no spinal cord or nerve roots in the sac. Associated anomalies are possible but do not define it.
notes.C: In an open myelocoele, the unfused neural placode can appear as an exposed raw plate without a raised meningeal sac.
notes.D: Myelocoele involves abnormal exposed neural tissue and can produce neurological deficits. The cord and nerves are not normally developed there.

questions.why: A meningocoele is a cerebrospinal fluid-containing protrusion of meninges without neural tissue in the sac. Myelocoele leaves the abnormal neural placode exposed at the surface.

questions.stem: In the development of the brain the following parts develop from the indicated embryonic segments

options.label: A
options.text: The medulla oblongata derives from the dorsal part of the metencephalon

options.label: B
options.text: The pons develops from the ventral part of the metencephalon

options.label: C
options.text: The third ventricle forms in the cavity of the diencephalon and part of the cavity in the telecephalon

options.label: D
options.text: The cerebral aqueduct develops from the cavity of the mesencephalon

options.label: E
options.text: The hippocampus develops in the wall of the telencephalon

notes.A: The medulla derives from the myelencephalon. The metencephalon forms the pons and cerebellum.
notes.B: The pons forms ventrally within the metencephalon, while the cerebellar primordium develops dorsally.
notes.C: The third ventricle is primarily diencephalic. Classical accounts also include a small midline telencephalic contribution at its rostral end.
notes.D: The mesencephalic lumen persists as the cerebral aqueduct linking the third and fourth ventricles.
notes.E: The hippocampal formation develops in the medial telencephalic wall as part of the cerebral pallium.

questions.why: The hindbrain subdivisions form the pons and medulla at different levels. Farther rostrally, the mesencephalic cavity persists as the aqueduct and forebrain cavities become the lateral and third ventricles.

questions.stem: All the following arise from neural crest cells, EXCEPT:
questions.why: The adrenal cortex develops from mesodermal coelomic epithelial cells. The adrenal medulla is developmentally distinct and is populated by chromaffin cells of neural crest lineage.

notes.A: Spinal sensory ganglion neurons are neural crest derivatives and lie in the dorsal root ganglia.
notes.B: Schwann cells are neural crest derivatives that associate with axons in peripheral nerves.
notes.C: Neural crest-derived melanoblasts migrate and differentiate into melanocytes in tissues such as the epidermis.
notes.D: Chromaffin cells are adrenal medullary derivatives of the neural crest lineage and release catecholamines.

questions.stem: Histopathological examination of a biopsy of a swelling in the midline of the v-shaped junction between the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of a patient’s tongue revealed normal thyroid tissue. Which of the following explains the presence of thyroid in the tongue?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of the thyroid primordium to descend from the foramen caecum

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of the mucous membrane of the posterior one-third of the tongue to cover the thyroid primordium

options.label: C
options.text: Maldescent of the thyroid primordium from the hypobranchial eminence

questions.why: The thyroid primordium originates in the midline pharyngeal floor near the future foramen caecum. Failure of its normal descent can leave thyroid tissue at the tongue base.

notes.B: Altered mucosal covering would not account for the thyroid remaining at its early position. The gland normally descends into the neck.
notes.C: The hypobranchial eminence forms part of the posterior tongue. The thyroid begins as a distinct median endodermal primordium.
notes.D: Location at the foramen caecum is explained by persistence along the normal thyroid pathway, without requiring abnormal lingual covering.
notes.E: The midline location is a recognised site of thyroid ectopia because it corresponds to the primordium’s site of origin.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the floor (depth) of the stomodeum?
questions.why: The stomodeum is the early ectodermal depression of the mouth. Its deep boundary is the buccopharyngeal membrane, which breaks down to open into the foregut.

notes.A: The pericardial region lies caudal to the developing mouth. It does not separate the oral depression from the foregut.
notes.B: The frontonasal process lies above the stomodeum and contributes to the forehead and nose.
notes.C: Lateral nasal prominences form later around the nasal pits. They are not the membrane at the bottom of the oral depression.
notes.D: The developing forebrain lies superior to the stomodeum. The deep oral boundary is a separate endoderm–ectoderm interface.

questions.stem: Which of the following arises by proliferation of mesenchyme on the ventral surface of the developing brain?
questions.why: Mesenchyme covering the ventral aspect of the forebrain expands into the frontonasal prominence. This median facial primordium forms the upper border of the developing mouth.

notes.B: The buccopharyngeal membrane is an epithelial boundary where ectoderm and endoderm meet, rather than a mesenchymal prominence.
notes.C: The maxillary processes are paired outgrowths of the first pharyngeal arch and border the stomodeum laterally.
notes.D: The mandibular processes are paired first-arch structures and form the lower border of the developing mouth.
notes.E: The stomodeum is a depression between facial prominences. It is not a mesenchymal outgrowth from the forebrain region.

questions.stem: Which of the underlisted structures does not contribute to the formation of the upper lip?
questions.why: The upper lip is formed by the two medial nasal prominences and the paired maxillary prominences; the lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose, not the lip, so they are the exception.

notes.A: Contributes.
notes.B: Contribute.
notes.D: Forms the philtrum.
notes.E: One is correct.

questions.stem: Which is the structure whose formation is directly associated with the appearance of the medial and lateral nasal prominences?
questions.why: Each nasal placode invaginates into a nasal pit. The mesenchyme bordering its medial and lateral edges grows into the paired medial and lateral nasal prominences.

notes.A: The frontonasal process carries the placodes, but the pits provide the immediate landmarks around which the nasal prominences appear.
notes.C: The lens placode forms where the optic vesicle contacts surface ectoderm. It is separate from the nasal placode and pit.
notes.D: The philtrum forms after the paired medial nasal prominences merge. It is a later component of the upper lip.
notes.E: The upper lip forms after fusion of facial prominences, including the medial nasal and maxillary components.

questions.stem: Which of the following forms the forehead during development of the face?

options.label: B
options.text: Middle narrow part of the frontonasal process

questions.why: The upper frontal region of the frontonasal prominence forms the forehead. The lower part carries the nasal placodes and contributes to development of the nose.

notes.B: The central lower part of the frontonasal prominence contributes to the nasal region. The forehead is derived more superiorly.
notes.C: The medial nasal prominences merge to form midline nasal structures and the intermaxillary segment, including the philtral component.
notes.D: The lateral nasal prominences contribute to the alae of the nose. They do not extend into the forehead.
notes.E: The philtrum is the midline contour of the upper lip and forms from the merged medial nasal prominences.

questions.stem: From the developmental account of how the face forms in the embryo, which of the following forms the bridge of the nose?

options.label: D
options.text: Terminal part of frontonasal process between medial nasal processes on either side

options.label: E
options.text: Middle narrow part of the frontonasal process

questions.why: The narrow middle part of the frontonasal process forms the bridge of the nose.

notes.A: Alae.
notes.B: Tip and philtrum.
notes.C: Forms the pit.
notes.D: Philtrum region.

questions.stem: Of the primordial structures that form the face in embryonic development, from which do the cheeks develop?

options.label: A
options.text: Upper broad part of frontonasal process

options.label: B
options.text: Middle narrow part of the frontonasal process

options.label: D
options.text: Lateral nasal process on either side

options.label: E
options.text: Fused lateral nasal and maxillary processes on either side

questions.why: The paired maxillary prominences expand laterally around the developing mouth and contribute to the cheeks. They also form much of the upper jaw and lateral upper lip.

notes.A: The upper frontonasal prominence forms the forehead and lies above the areas developing into the cheeks.
notes.B: The central frontonasal region forms part of the nose. The cheeks develop from a first-arch prominence on each side.
notes.D: Lateral nasal prominences contribute to the nasal alae. The adjacent cheek mesenchyme is mainly maxillary in origin.
notes.E: The lateral nasal–maxillary boundary is associated with the nasolacrimal groove. The cheeks arise principally from maxillary prominences.

questions.stem: The hard palate develops from which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Posterior outgrowths of the lateral palatal processes

options.label: E
options.text: Fused posterior outgrowths of the lateral palatal processes

questions.why: The primary palate forms anterior to the incisive foramen. The fused secondary palatal shelves contribute most of the remaining hard palate and continue posteriorly into the soft palate.

notes.A: The primary palate contributes the small premaxillary region anterior to the incisive foramen. Most of the hard palate is posterior to it.
notes.B: The secondary palate supplies most of the hard palate, but the primary palate contributes the anterior premaxillary part.
notes.D: Posterior regions of the palatal shelves contribute to the soft palate. Most hard palate forms from more anterior ossifying tissue.
notes.E: Fusion of posterior shelf tissue helps form the soft palate. The complete hard palate includes the primary palate as well.

questions.stem: The nasal septum develops from:
questions.why: The nasal septum grows inferiorly from the midline frontonasal tissue. It divides the nasal cavity and joins the developing palatal structures along the midline.

notes.B: The philtrum is an external midline feature of the upper lip. It is separate from the internal nasal partition.
notes.C: Lateral palatal shelves arise from the maxillary prominences. They meet the septum during fusion but do not form it.
notes.D: The septum has a frontonasal origin. Neither the philtrum nor the lateral palatal shelves is its source.
notes.E: The frontonasal prominence supplies the midline tissue that extends down to become the nasal septum.

questions.stem: The cells that produce dentin in the developing tooth differentiate from which of the following?
questions.why: Peripheral cells of the neural crest-derived dental papilla differentiate into odontoblasts and deposit dentine. The central region of the papilla becomes the dental pulp.

notes.A: The dental lamina forms tooth germs from oral epithelium. It does not provide the mesenchymal cells that produce dentine.
notes.B: Outer dental epithelium is the outer boundary of the enamel organ. Odontoblasts arise in the adjacent dental papilla.
notes.C: Inner dental epithelium gives rise to ameloblasts, the cells that produce enamel facing the developing dentine.
notes.D: The stellate reticulum is an epithelial support network of the enamel organ. It does not differentiate into odontoblasts.

questions.stem: The cells that produce enamel in the developing tooth differentiate from which of the following?
questions.why: Inner dental epithelial cells differentiate into ameloblasts at the enamel organ’s interface with the dental papilla. The ameloblasts deposit enamel on the developing dentine surface.

notes.A: The dental lamina is the epithelial precursor of the tooth germ. The immediate source of ameloblasts is the inner enamel epithelium.
notes.B: Outer dental epithelium forms the outer surface of the enamel organ. Ameloblasts differentiate on its inner surface.
notes.D: The stellate reticulum supports the enamel organ and helps maintain its shape. It is not the secretory ameloblast layer.
notes.E: The dental papilla supplies odontoblasts for dentine and cells of the pulp. Enamel is made by an epithelial lineage.

questions.stem: The musculature of the tongue arises from which of the following?
questions.why: Most tongue muscles arise from migrating occipital myotome cells and retain hypoglossal innervation. Palatoglossus is a pharyngeal arch muscle and has vagal innervation.

notes.A: The lateral lingual swellings form much of the mucosa of the anterior tongue. Their surface contribution is separate from muscle origin.
notes.B: The tuberculum impar is a median first-arch swelling. It is largely overgrown by the paired lateral swellings.
notes.D: The copula is an early midline swelling that is overgrown during posterior tongue development. It does not supply the main muscle lineage.
notes.E: The hypobranchial eminence contributes to mucosal regions of the posterior tongue. Most tongue muscle comes from migrating myotomes.

questions.stem: The mucous membrane of the posterior one-third of the tongue develops from which of the following?
questions.why: The posterior third of the tongue develops mainly from the third-arch part of the hypobranchial eminence. The more caudal fourth-arch region contributes near the epiglottis.

notes.A: The paired lateral lingual swellings are first-arch structures that form most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
notes.B: The tuberculum impar lies between the lateral lingual swellings and is overgrown as the anterior tongue forms.
notes.C: Occipital myotomes supply most tongue muscles. The surface mucosa of the posterior region comes from pharyngeal arch swellings.
notes.D: The second-arch copula is overgrown by the hypobranchial eminence, which forms most of the posterior mucosa.

questions.stem: A young mother reported to her paediatrician that each of her baby’s teeth that erupted had a smaller tooth on its lingual side. Which is the explanation for the baby’s condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Duplication of the dental lamina in each jaw

options.label: B
options.text: Excessive proliferation of cells in each dental bud

options.label: C
options.text: Abnormal cleavage of each dental bud

options.label: D
options.text: Precocious development of the bud for the permanent tooth

options.label: E
options.text: Incomplete development of the bud for the permanent tooth

questions.why: Permanent tooth buds form lingual to the deciduous ones; early development gives a double row.

notes.A: Not described.
notes.B: No.
notes.C: No.
notes.E: Would give missing teeth.

questions.stem: A young mother was alarmed to find that her newborn baby had bilateral cleft upper lip. What is the embryological explanation for the baby’s condition?

options.label: A
options.text: The frontonasal process failed to form during development of the face

options.label: B
options.text: There was a failure of fusion between the philtrum and the maxillary process on right side

options.label: C
options.text: There was a failure of fusion between the philtrum and the maxillary process on the left side

options.label: D
options.text: There was a failure of fusion between the lateral nasal process and the maxillary process on the right side

options.label: E
options.text: There was a failure of fusion between the lateral nasal process and the maxillary process of the left side

options.label: F
options.text: There was a failure of fusion between the medial nasal process and the maxillary process on the right side

options.label: G
options.text: There was a failure of fusion of the medial nasal process and the maxillary process on the left side

options.label: H
options.text: There was malfusion of the medial nasal processes in the formation of the philtrum

notes.A: The frontonasal prominence normally gives rise to the medial nasal structures. Bilateral clefts can occur with these structures present.
notes.B: On the right, failure of union between the maxillary prominence and the future philtral segment leaves a cleft beside the midline.
notes.C: The same failed junction on the left leaves the other cleft, separating the central segment from the lateral lip.
notes.D: The lateral nasal–maxillary junction is associated with the nasolacrimal groove, which is not the usual cleft-lip site.
notes.E: On the left, failure at the lateral nasal junction would involve a more lateral facial boundary near the nasolacrimal tract.
notes.F: The right maxillary prominence must join medial nasal-derived tissue to complete the right side of the upper lip.
notes.G: Failure of the corresponding left maxillary–medial nasal union produces the left-sided defect in a bilateral cleft.
notes.H: Failure of the two medial nasal prominences to join affects the midline. A typical bilateral cleft instead flanks the central segment.

questions.why: A typical bilateral cleft upper lip reflects failure of union on both sides between the maxillary prominences and the medial nasal-derived intermaxillary segment that forms the philtrum.

questions.stem: Evaluate the following statements concerning coincidence of cleft lip and palate in a baby

options.label: A
options.text: More males are affected than females

options.label: B
options.text: Affected females have a higher likelihood of having offspring with the same anomaly

options.label: C
options.text: Affected babies have serious feeding problems

options.label: D
options.text: If left untreated, improper speech habits will be acquired

options.label: E
options.text: Teeth development is impaired in affected babies

notes.A: About 2:1.
notes.B: The less-often-affected sex carries a higher recurrence risk.
notes.E: An alveolar cleft disturbs the teeth.

questions.why: All are true: cleft lip/palate is commoner in males, an affected mother has a higher chance of an affected child, and if untreated it causes feeding difficulty, defective speech habits and impaired tooth development.

questions.stem: Which of the following problems may be presented by a baby born with a severe cleft palate?

options.label: B
options.text: Regurgitation of suckled breast milk through the nose

options.label: C
options.text: Aspiration of suckled breast milk into the lungs

notes.D: Not usual.
notes.E: Not usual.

questions.why: A severe cleft palate causes difficulty suckling, nasal regurgitation of milk and aspiration into the lungs (A-C true); it does not impair crying or breathing, so D and E are false.

questions.stem: What are the external constrictions that separate bars of pharyngeal arches called?
questions.why: Pharyngeal clefts are the surface ectodermal grooves between neighbouring arches. Internal endodermal pockets are the pharyngeal pouches, which meet the clefts at thin intervening membranes.

notes.B: A pharyngeal membrane lies where a pouch and cleft approach one another. The external indentation itself is the cleft.
notes.C: Pouches are endoderm-lined pockets projecting from the inside of the embryonic pharynx between arches.
notes.D: The cervical sinus forms when the second arch grows over more caudal clefts. It is not the general term for the external grooves.
notes.E: Stenosis describes narrowing of a lumen. The normal surface boundaries between pharyngeal arches are grooves.

questions.stem: What structure does the first pharyngeal (hyomandibular) cleft give rise to?
questions.why: The first pharyngeal cleft is the ectodermal groove between the first and second arches. Classically it contributes the external acoustic meatus toward the tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The auditory tube is derived from the endodermal tubotympanic recess of the first pouch, on the internal side.
notes.B: The auricle forms from hillocks around the first cleft, with contributions from the first and second arches.
notes.D: The malleus is a derivative of a skeletal condensation of the first pharyngeal arch rather than from the surface groove.
notes.E: The tympanic membrane has several tissue layers, including outer ectoderm at the first-cleft boundary. The cleft’s canal derivative is the meatus.

questions.stem: Which anomaly of pharyngeal arch development has the synonyms: oculoauriculovertebral spectrum, Goldenhar syndrome, lateral facial dysplasia, first and second pharyngeal arch syndrome?
questions.why: Hemifacial microsomia is a presentation within the craniofacial microsomia spectrum, typically involving unilateral underdevelopment of first- and second-arch structures. Goldenhar describes overlapping oculoauriculovertebral features.

notes.B: Mandibulofacial dysostosis describes several syndromes, often with bilateral zygomatic and mandibular hypoplasia. It is distinct from typical hemifacial microsomia.
notes.C: Microtia is underdevelopment of the external ear. It can be a feature of this spectrum but names only one finding.
notes.D: Robin sequence involves a small mandible, posterior tongue displacement and airway obstruction. It is a different clinical pattern.
notes.E: Treacher Collins syndrome is a mandibulofacial dysostosis with frequently bilateral findings. The synonyms here point to the craniofacial microsomia spectrum.

questions.stem: Which is the primordial structure from which the mouth develops?
questions.why: The stomodeum is the primitive ectoderm-lined oral depression between developing facial prominences. It opens into the foregut after the buccopharyngeal membrane breaks down.

notes.A: The buccopharyngeal membrane temporarily separates the oral depression from the foregut and breaks down during development.
notes.B: Oropharyngeal membrane is another term for the transient partition at the depth of the oral depression.
notes.C: The stomodeal membrane is the temporary boundary at the base. The stomodeum itself is the primitive oral cavity.
notes.E: The proctodeum is the ectodermal depression at the caudal end of the gut and contributes to the lower anal canal.

questions.stem: Given that a patient has an abnormally large lower jaw, which of the following primordial structures of facial development is enlarged?
questions.why: The mandibular prominences arise from the first pharyngeal arches and supply the mesenchyme of the lower jaw. Excess lower-jaw growth corresponds to that developmental territory.

notes.B: The maxillary prominences form much of the upper jaw, cheeks and portions of the upper lip and palate.
notes.C: Medial nasal prominences contribute midline nasal and intermaxillary structures, including the philtral region of the upper lip.
notes.D: Lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose. They are separate from the lower jaw primordia.
notes.E: The frontonasal prominence forms the forehead and much of the nose. The lower jaw arises from paired first-arch prominences.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve is contained in the sixth pharyngeal arch?
questions.why: The sixth pharyngeal arch is associated with the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus. It supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles that differentiate within this arch territory.

notes.A: The cranial accessory designation is historically associated with fibres joining the vagus, but it does not name the sixth arch branch.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve is associated with the third arch and supplies its stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.C: Pharyngeal branches of the vagus help innervate the pharynx. The named sixth arch supply is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
notes.E: The superior laryngeal branch is associated with the fourth arch, including innervation of the cricothyroid muscle.

questions.stem: The mesoderm of the second pharyngeal arch gives rise to ALL the following EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: Part of the body of the hyoid bone

questions.why: Incus is 1st arch (Meckel's).

notes.B: 2nd.
notes.C: 2nd.
notes.D: 2nd.
notes.E: 2nd.

questions.stem: Which is the single muscle that develops in the mesenchyme of the third pharyngeal arch?
questions.why: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic muscle of the third pharyngeal arch. It retains glossopharyngeal innervation and elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing.

notes.A: Cricothyroid arises in the fourth arch territory and receives the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
notes.B: Levator veli palatini belongs to the fourth arch group in the classical account and is supplied through the pharyngeal plexus.
notes.C: The posterior digastric belly is a second-arch muscle and receives its motor supply from the facial nerve.
notes.D: Thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle supplied by cervical fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve. It is not a third-arch muscle.

questions.stem: Which of the following arise in common with the thymus from the endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch?
questions.why: The ventral third pharyngeal pouch forms thymic epithelium, and its dorsal portion forms the inferior parathyroids. Their descent explains why the third-pouch glands end up lower.

notes.B: Palatine tonsillar epithelium comes from the second pharyngeal pouch. Surrounding lymphoid cells populate it later.
notes.C: The pharyngeal tonsil develops in the roof of the nasopharynx. It is not paired with the thymus as a third-pouch derivative.
notes.D: The superior parathyroids are derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouches and migrate a shorter distance than the inferior glands.
notes.E: The ultimobranchial body is associated with the caudal pharyngeal pouch complex and joins the thyroid rather than the thymus.

questions.stem: Development of the face commences with the appearance of the olfactory placodes. In which of the following do the olfactory placodes appear?

options.label: E
options.text: Right and left medial nasal prominences

questions.why: Olfactory or nasal placodes are paired ectodermal thickenings on the lower frontonasal prominence. Their invagination establishes nasal pits and helps define adjacent nasal prominences.

notes.A: The buccopharyngeal membrane is a transient partition between the oral depression and foregut. It does not carry the nasal placodes.
notes.C: The philtrum develops later from merged medial nasal tissue and lies in the upper lip.
notes.D: Maxillary prominences flank the mouth and contribute to the upper jaw and lateral upper lip. The olfactory placodes lie higher.
notes.E: The medial nasal prominences form beside nasal pits after the olfactory placodes begin to invaginate.

questions.stem: A baby girl was born with normal external body structures, but she had an extremely small oral commissure. What is her condition called?
questions.why: Microstomia is an abnormally small oral opening. Congenital cases may reflect excessive union of the maxillary and mandibular facial components at the oral commissure.

notes.A: Hemifacial microsomia describes asymmetric underdevelopment of craniofacial structures, often including the mandible and ear.
notes.B: Möbius syndrome typically involves congenital facial weakness and impaired ocular abduction. It does not name a small oral opening.
notes.C: Mandibulofacial dysostosis describes a developmental pattern of facial skeletal abnormalities rather than the specific size of the mouth opening.
notes.D: Micrognathia describes a small jaw. The question identifies a small oral aperture at the commissure.

questions.stem: During development of the face, which of the following structures forms the lower boundary of the primitive mouth?
questions.why: The mandibular prominences of the first pharyngeal arch form the lower margin of the stomodeum. The maxillary prominences border it laterally, and the frontonasal prominence lies above.

notes.B: The maxillary process is also from the first arch, but it forms the side boundary of the primitive mouth.
notes.C: The lateral nasal prominence lies beside a nasal pit, superior to the first-arch lower margin of the stomodeum.
notes.D: The stomodeum is the primitive mouth depression. Its inferior margin is formed by the paired mandibular prominences.
notes.E: The buccopharyngeal membrane closes the deep boundary of the stomodeum, separating it from the underlying foregut.

questions.stem: The membrane closing the stomodeum, which breaks down at the end of week 4, is also called the:
questions.why: The oropharyngeal membrane, also called the buccopharyngeal membrane, initially separates the stomodeum from the foregut. It ruptures around the fourth week as the mouth opens.

notes.A: The cloacal membrane is at the caudal end of the embryonic gut, far from the oral depression.
notes.B: The laryngotracheal groove forms in ventral foregut and initiates respiratory development. It is not the oral boundary.
notes.C: The oesophagus forms farther caudally from dorsal foregut. Its opening does not name the membrane at the mouth.
notes.E: The proctodeum is an ectodermal depression at the caudal outlet. It contributes to the lower anal canal.

questions.stem: Early in facial development, the upper vertical length of the face is formed from which structure?
questions.why: The broad frontonasal process above the stomodeum supplies the early upper face. Its frontal region forms the forehead and its lower components contribute to the nose.

notes.A: Medial nasal processes arise around the nasal pits within the frontonasal region and form more local midline structures.
notes.B: Lateral nasal processes form at the outer edges of the nasal pits and contribute mainly to the alae.
notes.C: Maxillary processes lie on either side of the primitive mouth and contribute to the upper jaw and cheeks.
notes.D: Mandibular processes form the lower facial region, including the lower jaw and lower lip.

questions.stem: Transfacial cleft (macrostomia) results from failure of fusion of which structures?
questions.why: A transverse facial cleft causing macrostomia occurs when maxillary and mandibular prominences fail to unite normally at the lateral oral commissure. This widens the mouth opening.

notes.A: Failure at the medial nasal–maxillary junction produces a typical upper-lip cleft beside the philtrum.
notes.B: The lateral nasal–maxillary boundary follows the nasolacrimal groove. A defect there can produce an oblique facial cleft.
notes.D: Failure of the medial nasal prominences to unite can affect midline nasal or upper-lip structures, away from the oral commissure.
notes.E: A cleft due to failed union between mandibular prominences lies in the midline of the lower jaw or lip.

questions.stem: When a pregnant woman abuses alcohol, the baby is born with features of fetal alcohol syndrome (FASD). Which of the following is a feature?
questions.why: Short palpebral fissures are one of three characteristic facial findings used in assessment for fetal alcohol syndrome. The others are a smooth philtrum and thin upper vermilion.

notes.B: The characteristic lip finding is a thin upper vermilion border. Lip thickness is assessed with an appropriate reference guide.
notes.C: Nasal bridge shape can vary and is not a defining facial criterion. Short horizontal eyelid openings are a characteristic finding.
notes.D: A large mandible is not a characteristic feature. Some affected children have a small mandible or midface hypoplasia.
notes.E: Nasal width is not one of the characteristic diagnostic facial measurements. The palpebral fissures, philtrum and upper vermilion are assessed.

questions.stem: From the developmental account of how the face develops in the embryo, which of the following forms the lateral parts of the nose?
questions.why: Lateral nasal prominences form the outer borders of the early nasal pits and develop into the alae. The merged medial prominences contribute to the central nasal region.

notes.A: The medial processes contribute to central nasal structures and the intermaxillary segment. The alae are formed laterally.
notes.C: The maxillary processes form the cheeks and much of the upper jaw. They meet lateral nasal tissue near the nasolacrimal groove.
notes.D: Mandibular processes form the lower jaw and lower lip. They are not the immediate source of the nasal alae.
notes.E: The frontonasal process is the parent region. The lateral nasal prominences are its direct local derivatives forming the alae.

questions.stem: A cleft lip and palate results from failure of fusion of which structures?
questions.why: The upper lip and primary palate depend on union of maxillary tissue with the medial nasal-derived intermaxillary segment. Clefts extending into secondary palate also involve the palatal shelves.

notes.B: Failure at the lateral nasal–maxillary junction is associated with an oblique facial cleft near the nasolacrimal groove.
notes.C: The maxillary–mandibular junction forms the lateral oral commissure. Its failure leads to a transverse facial cleft or macrostomia.
notes.D: The frontonasal process contributes to the medial nasal prominences. The relevant junction is more specifically between medial nasal and maxillary tissue.
notes.E: Failure of the medial nasal prominences to unite affects midline facial development. A typical upper-lip cleft lies to one side of the midline.

questions.stem: Some individuals are born with inability to roll their tongue. Which structure forms the muscles of the tongue?
questions.why: Most tongue muscles arise from myotomes of the occipital somites. Their precursors migrate into the tongue and retain hypoglossal innervation, with palatoglossus a pharyngeal arch exception.

notes.B: Pharyngeal arch regions give rise to tongue mucosa and the arch muscle palatoglossus. Most intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles come from occipital myotomes.
notes.C: Neural crest cells contribute craniofacial connective tissues and other supporting structures. Tongue myofibres are mainly myotomal mesoderm.
notes.D: Endoderm contributes much of the posterior tongue’s epithelial lining. It does not supply the migrating muscle precursors.
notes.E: Ectoderm can contribute surface epithelium in the oral region. The tongue skeletal muscles do not arise from this lining.

questions.stem: A patient has loss of sense of taste. Which nerve supplies taste buds in the posterior third of the tongue?
questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. It also carries taste from circumvallate papillae near the boundary.

notes.A: The facial nerve carries taste from most of the anterior two-thirds through the chorda tympani.
notes.C: The vagus carries taste from the epiglottic region, farther caudally than the usual posterior lingual territory.
notes.D: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles. It does not carry taste from lingual taste buds.
notes.E: The lingual branch of the mandibular trigeminal nerve carries general sensation from the anterior tongue. Taste fibres travelling with it belong to the facial nerve.

questions.stem: Most thymus organs develop from the third pharyngeal pouch. What are the derivatives of the third pharyngeal pouch?
questions.why: Each third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to thymic epithelial tissue ventrally and an inferior parathyroid primordium dorsally. Both migrate caudally before separating.

notes.A: Thymic epithelium does develop from the ventral third pouch. Its dorsal companion is also a derivative.
notes.B: Inferior parathyroids develop from the dorsal third pouch, which also gives rise to the thymus ventrally.
notes.C: Palatine tonsillar epithelium arises from the second pouch. It is not part of the third-pouch pair.
notes.E: The inferior parathyroids are correctly included. Tonsillar tissue is the misplaced second-pouch derivative in this combination.

questions.stem: The third pharyngeal arch gives rise to which structure?
questions.why: The third pharyngeal arch contributes the greater horns and lower part of the hyoid body. The lesser horns arise from second-arch skeletal tissue.

notes.A: The stylohyoid ligament develops along the second-arch cartilage lineage. It connects the styloid process to the hyoid.
notes.C: The lesser horn is a second-arch derivative, along with the upper portion of the hyoid body in the classical account.
notes.D: Thyroid cartilage is part of the laryngeal skeleton, which develops from more caudal arch territories than the hyoid greater horns.
notes.E: Cricoid cartilage also belongs to the laryngeal skeleton and forms from caudal arch mesenchyme.

questions.stem: All of the following muscles develop from the 2nd arch (facial nerve) EXCEPT:
questions.why: Tensor tympani is a first-arch muscle supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Stapedius and the other listed second-arch muscles receive facial nerve supply.

notes.A: Stapedius is a second-arch muscle in the middle ear and receives a branch of the facial nerve.
notes.B: Stylohyoid is derived from the second arch and is innervated by the facial nerve.
notes.C: The posterior belly of digastric has second-arch origin and facial innervation. The anterior belly belongs to the first arch.
notes.E: Muscles of facial expression are derived from second-arch myoblasts and retain facial nerve innervation after migration.

questions.stem: The palatine tonsils derive from which of the following?
questions.why: Endoderm of the second pharyngeal pouch forms the epithelium and crypts of the palatine tonsil. Lymphoid cells subsequently populate the connective tissue around those crypts.

notes.A: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, which contributes to the auditory tube and middle ear.
notes.C: The third pouch gives rise to thymic epithelium and the inferior parathyroids. The palatine tonsil has a different pouch origin.
notes.D: The first arch forms structures such as the jaw primordia and muscles of mastication. Tonsillar epithelium is pouch endoderm.
notes.E: The second arch contributes facial expression muscles and hyoid-related skeletal structures. Its adjacent pouch has a distinct endodermal lineage.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the 2nd (hyoid) arch cartilage include the:

notes.A: The stapes superstructure is classically a second-arch derivative. The footplate has a more complex origin near the otic capsule.
notes.B: The stylohyoid ligament is associated with Reichert’s cartilage and runs between the styloid process and hyoid.
notes.C: The lesser horn belongs to the second-arch contribution to the hyoid. The greater horn is attributed to the third arch.
notes.D: The malleus is a first-arch ossicle associated with the proximal region of Meckel’s cartilage.
notes.E: The incus is also a first-arch ossicle, connecting the malleus to the stapes in the middle ear.

questions.why: The second arch skeletal primordium, Reichert’s cartilage, gives rise to structures including the stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn of the hyoid and much of the stapes.

questions.stem: Which congenital anomaly arises from incomplete fusion of lateral lingual swellings?
questions.why: The paired first-arch lateral lingual swellings normally unite at the midline. Incomplete merging can leave a bifid tongue with a cleft at its tip.

notes.A: Agnathia refers to absence of a jaw, usually the mandible. It does not describe separation of the anterior tongue.
notes.B: Ankyloglossia limits movement of the tongue because of its lingual frenulum. It does not create a bifid tip.
notes.D: Macroglossia is enlargement of the tongue, which can occur even when the lingual swellings fuse normally.
notes.E: Microglossia is an abnormally small tongue. Incomplete fusion characteristically produces a midline division instead.

questions.stem: The lateral lingual swellings that form the anterior two-thirds of the tongue derive from which arch?
questions.why: The paired lateral lingual swellings arise in the first pharyngeal arch. They enlarge and merge over the median tuberculum impar to form most of the anterior tongue mucosa.

notes.B: The second arch contributes the transient copula, which is overgrown during development of the posterior tongue.
notes.C: The third arch supplies much of the posterior third mucosa through the hypobranchial eminence.
notes.D: The fourth arch contributes to the most caudal tongue region near the epiglottis, farther back than the paired lateral swellings.
notes.E: The conventionally numbered fifth arch is rudimentary or absent in usual descriptions and supplies no anterior tongue swelling.

questions.stem: The lingual foramen cecum marks the origin of which organ?
questions.why: The foramen caecum marks the midline site where the thyroid primordium starts in the developing tongue. The thyroid normally descends through the neck from that region.

notes.A: The parathyroids arise from paired pharyngeal pouches, with inferior glands from the third and superior glands from the fourth.
notes.B: Palatine tonsillar epithelium is derived from the second pharyngeal pouch, at a lateral pharyngeal site.
notes.D: The thymic epithelium arises from the ventral third pouch and migrates toward the anterior mediastinum.
notes.E: The major salivary glands bud from oral epithelium at their own sites. The midline foramen is a landmark of the thyroid pathway.

questions.stem: Parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid arise from which structure?
questions.why: Thyroid parafollicular cells develop in the ultimobranchial body, a derivative of the caudal pharyngeal pouch complex. It joins the developing thyroid and supplies its calcitonin-secreting cells.

notes.A: The median thyroid diverticulum is the main primordium for follicular epithelium. The parafollicular cells reach it through the separate ultimobranchial body.
notes.B: The lateral lingual swellings form anterior tongue mucosa, far from the caudal pouch that contributes parafollicular cells.
notes.C: The tuberculum impar is a first-arch midline lingual swelling. It is separate from the migrating pouch-derived tissue.
notes.E: Vallate papillae are lingual taste-associated structures. They do not provide a lineage for thyroid endocrine cells.

questions.stem: The parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouches?
questions.why: Inferior parathyroids arise from the dorsal third pharyngeal pouches and descend with the thymus. Superior parathyroids arise from the fourth pouches and usually migrate a shorter distance.

notes.A: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, and the second gives rise to palatine tonsillar epithelium.
notes.B: The third pouch provides the inferior glands. The superior glands come from the fourth pouch rather than the second.
notes.D: The fourth pouch contributes only the superior set. The inferior set migrates from the third pouch.
notes.E: The first pouch forms the tubotympanic recess and does not give rise to the parathyroids.

questions.stem: Structures that develop from the pharyngeal gut include:

notes.A: Ameloblasts differentiate from oral ectoderm-derived dental epithelium. They secrete enamel rather than pharyngeal endoderm forming it.
notes.B: The posterior tongue mucosa is associated with pharyngeal arch endoderm. Much of the anterior oral lining has a different origin.
notes.C: The thyroid follicular primordium arises in the midline pharyngeal floor and descends into the neck.
notes.D: The parotid bud is classically described as an outgrowth of oral epithelium on the ectodermal side.
notes.E: Thymic epithelial cells arise from the ventral third pouch. Developing lymphocytes later populate that epithelial framework.

questions.why: Pharyngeal endoderm contributes to posterior tongue lining, the thyroid primordia and thymic epithelium. The developing mouth also contains ectodermal epithelium, which produces enamel and classically the parotid buds.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the FIRST pharyngeal arch include:

notes.A: The incus is a first-arch auditory ossicle, along with the malleus, associated with Meckel’s cartilage.
notes.B: The sphenomandibular ligament persists along the first-arch mandibular cartilage pathway between sphenoid and mandible.
notes.C: The posterior digastric belly belongs to the second arch and receives facial nerve supply. The anterior belly is first-arch derived.
notes.D: Mylohyoid is a first-arch muscle. Its nerve comes from the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular trigeminal division.
notes.E: Tensor veli palatini is innervated by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve, consistent with its first-arch origin.

questions.why: First-arch mesenchyme contributes jaw-associated skeletal structures and several muscles supplied by mandibular trigeminal fibres. This includes the incus, mylohyoid and tensor veli palatini.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the THIRD pharyngeal arch include:

notes.A: Stylohyoid belongs to the second-arch muscle group and is supplied by the facial nerve.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic third-arch muscle and receives branches from the glossopharyngeal nerve.
notes.C: The greater horn is a third-arch skeletal derivative. The lesser horn is classically attributed to the second arch.
notes.D: The styloid process is associated with Reichert’s cartilage of the second arch rather than the third arch.
notes.E: Palatopharyngeus develops in the more caudal pharyngeal muscle group and receives vagal fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.why: The third arch contributes the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid. Its characteristic muscle is stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

questions.stem: Derivatives of the FIRST pharyngeal pouch include the:

options.label: D
options.text: Inner (endodermal) layer of the tympanic membrane

notes.A: The expanded distal recess contributes to the tympanic cavity surrounding the developing ossicles.
notes.B: The mastoid antrum forms as an extension of the developing middle-ear space posteriorly.
notes.C: The tubotympanic recess is the elongating first-pouch outgrowth that establishes the tube and cavity.
notes.D: Endoderm from the first pouch forms the inner mucosal layer. The outer epithelial layer comes from surface ectoderm.
notes.E: The narrower proximal part of the recess persists as the auditory tube connecting the nasopharynx and tympanic cavity.

questions.why: The first pouch extends as the tubotympanic recess. Its lumen contributes the auditory tube and middle-ear space, and its endoderm forms the inner layer of the tympanic membrane.

questions.stem: Structures associated with the cervical sinus (2nd–4th clefts) include:

notes.A: The cervical sinus is the temporary recess created by overgrowth of the second pharyngeal arch over caudal clefts.
notes.B: A branchial cyst may develop when tissue lining the cervical sinus persists instead of regressing.
notes.C: Thymic epithelium arises from endoderm of the third pouch. The cervical sinus is a surface ectodermal feature.
notes.D: The superior parathyroid develops from the fourth pouch, an internal endodermal recess.
notes.E: The ultimobranchial body is derived from the caudal pouch complex and later joins the developing thyroid.

questions.why: The second arch overgrows the more caudal surface clefts and encloses a transient cervical sinus. Persistence of ectodermal remnants can produce a lateral cervical cyst.

questions.stem: About development of the face:

options.label: A
options.text: The philtrum comes from the medial nasal prominences

options.label: B
options.text: The nasolacrimal groove lies between the maxillary and LATERAL nasal prominences

options.label: C
options.text: The lateral nasal prominences do not contribute to the upper lip

options.label: D
options.text: The lower lip comes entirely from the mandibular prominences

options.label: E
options.text: The face is fully formed by about 10 weeks

notes.A: Merged medial nasal prominences form the intermaxillary segment, whose superficial labial component is the philtrum.
notes.B: The nasolacrimal groove separates the maxillary prominence from the lateral nasal prominence and contributes the drainage pathway.
notes.C: The lateral nasal prominences form the nasal alae. The upper lip is derived from medial nasal and maxillary tissue.
notes.D: The paired mandibular prominences unite in the midline and contribute the lower lip.
notes.E: By around ten weeks the principal facial features have formed. Growth and remodelling continue thereafter.

questions.why: The medial nasal prominences merge and contribute the philtrum, while maxillary tissue forms the lateral upper lip. Mandibular prominences unite below the mouth to form the lower lip.

questions.stem: Which structure on the surface of the limb bud maintains its distal outgrowth?
questions.why: The apical ectodermal ridge is a thickened band at the distal tip of the limb bud. Its fibroblast growth factors maintain proliferation of underlying mesenchyme and support outgrowth.

notes.B: Somatic lateral plate mesoderm supplies the limb bud mesenchyme. The surface ridge is an ectodermal signalling structure.
notes.C: Somitic mesoderm sends muscle precursors into the limb. It is not the distal surface tissue maintaining outgrowth.
notes.D: The posterior zone of polarising activity patterns the thumb-to-little-finger axis through Sonic hedgehog signalling.
notes.E: The underlying mesenchyme proliferates in response to signals. The named surface source of those signals is the ectodermal ridge.

questions.stem: Outgrowth of the forelimbs is induced by TBX5 and FGF10, whilst outgrowth of the hindlimbs is induced by TBX4 and FGF10. Which region in the limb bud controls proximal–distal growth in size?
questions.why: Once a limb bud has been initiated, growth along its proximal–distal axis depends on reciprocal signalling with the apical ectodermal ridge. Ridge-derived fibroblast growth factors sustain distal outgrowth.

notes.B: The zone of polarising activity lies posteriorly and patterns the anterior–posterior sequence of digits.
notes.C: The somatic mesodermal core produces several limb tissues and interacts with the ridge. The distal ectodermal ridge supplies the specific outgrowth signals.
notes.D: Ventral ectoderm contributes to dorsal–ventral patterning and helps position the ridge at the interface with dorsal ectoderm.
notes.E: Dorsal ectoderm provides positional signals for dorsal limb identity. The distal ridge maintains proximal–distal outgrowth.

questions.stem: During limb development, failure of separation of digits results in fused or webbed fingers and/or toes. Which of the following anomalies describes this condition?
questions.why: Syndactyly is persistent union of adjacent digits. Failure of normal regression of interdigital tissue can leave soft-tissue webbing, and some forms also include fusion of bones.

notes.B: Ectrodactyly involves absence of one or more digits or rays, often with a central cleft in the hand or foot.
notes.C: Polydactyly causes one or more extra digits. It is distinct from continued attachment between adjacent digits.
notes.D: Brachydactyly describes abnormally short digits, usually because of shortened bones in the hand or foot.
notes.E: Symbrachydactyly features short or absent digits and can also include webbing. The stated isolated separation defect is syndactyly.

questions.stem: A baby has total absence of one lower limb. The term is:
questions.why: Amelia is complete absence of one or more limbs. When some limb components are present and other parts are missing, terminology depends on the pattern of partial absence.

notes.B: Hemimelia denotes a partial limb deficiency. Complete absence of the entire limb is a different category.
notes.C: Meromelia describes partial absence of a limb, with at least some structures such as a proximal or distal segment present.
notes.D: Phocomelia is a severe limb reduction in which hands or feet can remain close to the trunk despite shortened or absent long bones.
notes.E: Sirenomelia is fusion and malformation of the lower limbs, often with associated internal abnormalities.

questions.stem: How long after the upper limb buds do the lower limb buds appear?

options.label: E
options.text: They appear at the same time

questions.why: Upper limb buds become visible first in the fourth week. Lower limb buds appear shortly afterward, typically about two days later in the standard developmental sequence.

notes.B: The visible lower buds follow within the same general fourth-week window, so a full week is longer than the usual interval.
notes.C: By two weeks after upper limb budding, the lower limbs are already in further stages of growth and patterning.
notes.D: Four weeks later the limbs are much more advanced. The initial upper and lower buds emerge days apart.
notes.E: The upper buds become visible first. Lower buds follow shortly afterward, with timing varying somewhat by embryonic stage.

questions.stem: The usefulness of embryology to a medical student includes ALL of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Provision of rational explanation for the position of many normal adult structures

options.label: B
options.text: Knowledge of development and relationship of foetal membranes facilitates their study in obstetrics

options.label: C
options.text: Facilitation of understanding of congenital abnormalities

options.label: D
options.text: Understanding of hormonal deficiencies in people

questions.why: Embryology explains how normal anatomy, fetal membranes and congenital abnormalities develop. Hormonal deficiencies as a general subject are addressed more directly through physiology and clinical endocrinology.

notes.A: Embryonic development helps explain the adult positions of the testes and the courses of the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
notes.B: Study of fetal membranes and placental relationships provides a foundation for obstetrics and perinatal anatomy.
notes.C: Congenital abnormalities often reflect deviations from normal development, so embryology helps explain their anatomical patterns.
notes.E: Embryology connects microscopic tissue differentiation with gross anatomy, providing context across the morphological disciplines.

questions.stem: Which is the stem cell in the spermatogenic lineage?
questions.why: The spermatogonial stem-cell pool is in the type A population near the seminiferous tubule basement membrane. It self-renews and generates progenitors that enter the differentiating pathway.

notes.A: Spermatids are haploid products of meiosis. They differentiate into spermatozoa without renewing the basal germ-cell pool.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are committed differentiating cells that produce primary spermatocytes. They follow the renewing type A population.
notes.D: Primary spermatocytes enter the first meiotic division. They are downstream of mitotically active spermatogonia.
notes.E: Secondary spermatocytes form after meiosis I and enter meiosis II. They have already left the mitotic stem-cell stage.

questions.stem: Which is the hormone directly responsible for ovulation?
questions.why: The mid-cycle luteinising hormone surge directly triggers follicular rupture and oocyte release. It also promotes resumption of oocyte meiosis and luteinisation of the remaining follicular cells.

notes.A: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone controls pituitary gonadotrophin secretion. The pituitary luteinising hormone surge acts directly on the ovary.
notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone supports follicle growth and granulosa cell function. It is not the principal direct trigger for rupture.
notes.D: Sustained preovulatory oestradiol causes positive feedback leading to the luteinising hormone surge. Its role is upstream of follicular rupture.
notes.E: Progesterone rises after luteinisation and acts on the endometrium. It is not the main trigger for ovulation.

questions.stem: Which hormone is directly responsible for the maintenance of the corpus luteum of menstruation?
questions.why: Pituitary luteinising hormone supports steroid production by the corpus luteum during the menstrual cycle. In early pregnancy, human chorionic gonadotrophin provides the signal that rescues it from regression.

notes.A: Follicle-stimulating hormone mainly supports the growing follicle. Luteal steroid production depends more directly on luteinising hormone.
notes.C: Human chorionic gonadotrophin is produced after implantation and maintains the corpus luteum of early pregnancy rather than the ordinary cycle.
notes.D: Human chorionic somatomammotrophin is placental lactogen. It has metabolic and mammary effects and does not sustain the menstrual corpus luteum.
notes.E: Placental thyroid-stimulating activity is distinct from luteotrophic signalling. Pituitary luteinising hormone is the relevant support in the non-pregnant cycle.

questions.stem: The following statements are correct in respect of oogenesis

options.label: A
options.text: There is no mitotic division in the gametes after birth

options.label: B
