options.text: All oocytes present after birth have commenced the first meiotic division

options.label: C
options.text: The process is never permanently terminated in a lifetime

options.label: D
options.text: The primary oocyte in a primordial follicle contains 23 chromosomes

options.label: E
options.text: The secondary oocyte released at ovulation contains 23 pairs of chromosomes

options.label: F
options.text: The secondary oocyte released at ovulation contains fourfold the amount of DNA (4N) in a haploid cell

options.label: G
options.text: The second meiotic division of the secondary oocyte (ovum) is not necessary since it already contains only 23 chromosomes

options.label: H
options.text: The polar bodies released at each meiotic division contain 46 chromosomes each

options.label: I
options.text: The female pronucleus produced after the second meiotic division of the secondary oocyte (ovum) determines the genetic sex of the foetus

options.label: J
options.text: The secondary oocyte (ovum) released at ovulation has either Y- or X-bearing chromosome

options.label: K
options.text: The secondary oocyte (ovum) released at ovulation remains viable in the ovarian tubes for 14 days

notes.A: Mitotic proliferation of oogonia normally occurs prenatally. The postnatal oocyte pool consists of cells already committed to meiosis.
notes.B: Oocytes in neonatal primordial follicles have entered meiosis I and are arrested in its prophase.
notes.C: The finite ovarian reserve declines largely through atresia. Reproductive ovulatory cycles generally cease at menopause.
notes.D: A primary oocyte is diploid with 46 chromosomes. After DNA replication each chromosome comprises two sister chromatids.
notes.E: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosome pairs. A secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes, each still having two sister chromatids.
notes.F: The secondary oocyte is haploid in chromosome sets with twice the DNA content of a mature haploid gamete, not fourfold.
notes.G: Meiosis II separates the remaining sister chromatids and allows extrusion of the second polar body after activation.
notes.H: Polar bodies produced by normal oocyte meiosis are haploid. Their chromosomes are duplicated after the first division and unduplicated after the second.
notes.I: The maternal pronucleus normally provides an X chromosome. The fertilising sperm normally provides either X or Y.
notes.J: A typical secondary oocyte contains one X chromosome and no Y chromosome. X–Y variation usually comes from sperm.
notes.K: The ovulated oocyte is generally fertilisable for roughly a day. Fourteen days is closer to the length of a typical luteal phase.

questions.why: Human oocytes enter meiosis before birth and arrest in prophase I. The ovulated secondary oocyte has 23 duplicated chromosomes and normally finishes meiosis II only after fertilisation.

questions.stem: Concerning the cells in the spermatogenic lineage, the following statements are correct

options.label: M
options.text: Spermatids undergo cytodifferentiation known as spermiogenesis

options.label: N
options.text: When type-A spermatogonia divide they produce both type-A and type-B spermatogonia

options.label: O
options.text: When type-B spermatogonia divide they produce primary spermatocytes

options.label: P
options.text: Primary spermatocytes produce spermatids when they divide

options.label: Q
options.text: Spermatids produce secondary spermatocytes when they divide

options.label: R
options.text: Spermatozoa in the epididymis multiply by mitotic division

notes.A: Spermatids have 23 chromosomes after meiosis II, which separates the sister chromatids of secondary spermatocytes.
notes.B: A typical human spermatozoon is haploid and carries 23 chromosomes, including one sex chromosome.
notes.C: A primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. After premeiotic DNA replication these consist of paired sister chromatids.
notes.D: Secondary spermatocytes have 23 chromosomes after homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I.
notes.E: Type A spermatogonia are diploid and have 46 chromosomes before they give rise to differentiating descendants.
notes.F: Type B spermatogonia also have 46 chromosomes and still belong to the diploid mitotic compartment.
notes.G: The type A population undergoes mitosis, supporting both renewal and production of differentiating germ-cell progenitors.
notes.H: Type B spermatogonia divide mitotically. Their primary spermatocyte descendants undergo the first meiotic division.
notes.I: Primary spermatocytes are committed to meiosis I, which separates homologues rather than sister chromatids.
notes.J: Secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis II, separating sister chromatids and producing haploid spermatids.
notes.K: Spermatids have completed meiosis. They remodel their nuclei, cytoplasm and flagellar apparatus during spermiogenesis.
notes.L: A spermatozoon is the mature product of spermatogenesis and does not restart that developmental programme.
notes.M: Spermiogenesis is the differentiation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon without a further cell division.
notes.N: The type A population includes renewing cells and differentiating progenitors, whose descendants give rise to type B spermatogonia.
notes.O: Type B spermatogonia undergo their final mitotic divisions before their descendants differentiate into primary spermatocytes.
notes.P: Meiosis I of a primary spermatocyte first produces secondary spermatocytes. Spermatids are the next meiotic products.
notes.Q: Secondary spermatocytes give rise to spermatids through meiosis II. Spermatids do not divide to reverse that sequence.
notes.R: Epididymal sperm undergo functional maturation and storage, while mitotic proliferation is restricted to earlier spermatogonia in the testis.

questions.why: Diploid spermatogonia proliferate by mitosis and give rise to primary spermatocytes. Meiosis produces haploid spermatids, which remodel into spermatozoa without any further division.

questions.stem: Which cell undergoes the second meiotic division?
questions.why: A secondary spermatocyte forms after meiosis I and has one set of duplicated chromosomes. It completes meiosis II to separate sister chromatids and form spermatids.

notes.A: The primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I, which separates homologous chromosomes and forms secondary spermatocytes.
notes.C: A spermatid is the product of meiosis II and differentiates without another division during spermiogenesis.
notes.D: Type B spermatogonia undergo mitotic division and are the precursors of primary spermatocytes.
notes.E: A spermatozoon is a terminally differentiated haploid cell. It is produced by spermiogenesis rather than another meiotic division.

questions.stem: Which cell results from mitotic division of a type B spermatogonium?
questions.why: Type B spermatogonia are committed diploid germ cells. After their final mitotic divisions, the descendants differentiate into primary spermatocytes and enter the first meiotic division.

notes.B: Secondary spermatocytes are formed only after primary spermatocytes complete meiosis I and separate their homologous chromosomes.
notes.C: Spermatids are postmeiotic cells formed when secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II.
notes.D: Type B spermatogonia are the precursor population named in the question. Their differentiating descendants enter the primary spermatocyte stage.
notes.E: A spermatozoon forms by remodelling a spermatid after both meiotic divisions, well downstream of spermatogonial mitosis.

questions.stem: Which cell undergoes spermiogenesis?
questions.why: Spermiogenesis transforms a haploid spermatid into a spermatozoon without division. The nucleus condenses, an acrosome and flagellum develop, and much of the excess cytoplasm is lost.

notes.B: Secondary spermatocytes complete meiosis II to produce spermatids. Those spermatids are the cells that subsequently remodel.
notes.C: Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I and produce secondary spermatocytes. The sperm-shaped stage comes later.
notes.D: A spermatozoon is the product of spermiogenesis. It undergoes later functional maturation in the epididymis.
notes.E: Type A spermatogonia belong to the early mitotic population and provide progenitors for the meiotic lineage.

questions.stem: Which daughter cell of oocyte meiosis has very little cytoplasm?
questions.why: Meiotic cytokinesis in oogenesis is unequal. A small polar body receives chromosomes and little cytoplasm, while the larger daughter retains the cytoplasm needed to support early development.

notes.B: The secondary oocyte receives most of the cytoplasm during meiosis I, leaving little for the first polar body.
notes.C: The primary oocyte is the large precursor that enters meiosis I. It is not the small meiotic daughter.
notes.D: The ootid is the large functional product after meiosis II. The second polar body receives much less cytoplasm.
notes.E: Oogonia are prenatal mitotic germ cells. They precede primary oocytes and are not products of meiotic cytokinesis.

questions.stem: Which cell is discharged at ovulation?
questions.why: By ovulation, the primary oocyte has usually completed meiosis I and expelled its first polar body. The ovary releases the secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II.

notes.B: A primary oocyte retains homologous chromosome pairs and precedes completion of meiosis I. The ovulated cell has passed this stage.
notes.C: The ootid forms when meiosis II is completed, normally after sperm entry activates the ovulated secondary oocyte.
notes.D: The first polar body can remain under the zona pellucida, but the functional cell released is the secondary oocyte.
notes.E: Oogonia proliferate during fetal ovarian development and give rise to primary oocytes long before ovulation begins.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates follicular maturation at puberty?
questions.why: Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on granulosa cells and supports maturation of growing ovarian follicles. Later in the cycle a luteinising hormone surge directly triggers ovulation.

notes.B: Luteinising hormone acts on theca cells and triggers ovulation in a surge. Follicle-stimulating hormone directly supports granulosa growth.
notes.C: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone acts on the pituitary to release follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormones, rather than acting directly on follicles.
notes.D: Oestrogen is produced by growing follicles and provides feedback to the reproductive axis. It is not the pituitary follicle-stimulating signal.
notes.E: Progesterone derives predominantly from the luteal phase corpus luteum. Its major cyclic role is supporting secretory endometrium.

questions.stem: A primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of cuboidal follicular cells is a:
questions.why: During the transition from primordial to primary follicle, the flattened follicular cells become cuboidal. A single cuboidal layer identifies the unilaminar stage before granulosa cells proliferate further.

notes.A: Primordial follicles have a single layer of flattened follicular cells. Cuboidal cells indicate activation into a primary follicle.
notes.C: A multilaminar primary follicle has several granulosa cell layers rather than a single layer.
notes.D: An antral follicle has a fluid-filled space within the granulosa cell layers, a later developmental feature.
notes.E: A Graafian follicle is a large preovulatory antral follicle. Its cavity and granulosa organisation go beyond the single cuboidal layer.

questions.stem: Which hormone is produced by the granulosa and theca cells of a growing follicle?
questions.why: Growing follicles produce oestrogen through cooperation between two cell types. Theca cells supply androgen substrate, and granulosa-cell aromatase converts it to oestradiol under follicle-stimulating hormone influence.

notes.B: Progesterone becomes the predominant luteal steroid after ovulation. The characteristic cooperative product of the growing follicle is oestradiol.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone comes from the anterior pituitary and stimulates theca androgen synthesis. It is a signal to the follicle.
notes.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone is a pituitary gonadotrophin. It promotes granulosa aromatase activity rather than being made by follicular cells.
notes.E: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone is produced by the hypothalamus and controls pituitary gonadotrophin release upstream of ovarian steroid synthesis.

questions.stem: A primary oocyte surrounded by several layers of granulosa cells is a:
questions.why: Several layers of granulosa cells around the oocyte define a multilaminar primary follicle.

notes.A: Single flat layer of follicular cells.
notes.B: One layer of cuboidal cells.
notes.D: First antrum appears.
notes.E: Large antrum fills most of it.

questions.stem: The first follicle in which an antrum appears is the:
questions.why: An antrum begins when small fluid pockets within the granulosa layer coalesce. In the terminology used here this transition identifies the secondary, or antral, follicle.

notes.A: A primordial follicle has a primary oocyte and one surrounding layer of flattened cells. Its small structure has no antrum.
notes.B: The unilaminar primary stage has one cuboidal follicular cell layer before a fluid cavity develops.
notes.C: A multilaminar primary follicle is preantral in this classification, even though it has several granulosa layers.
notes.E: The Graafian follicle has a large, established antrum. The cavity first appears earlier during antral development.

questions.stem: A follicle in which follicular fluid fills most of the space is the:
questions.why: The antrum occupies most of a mature Graafian follicle. The oocyte is displaced toward the periphery and remains attached to the granulosa wall through the cumulus oophorus.

notes.A: A primordial follicle has flattened supporting cells around the oocyte and no fluid-filled antrum.
notes.B: A unilaminar primary follicle has one layer of cuboidal cells and has not yet developed a fluid cavity.
notes.C: The multilaminar primary stage adds several granulosa layers, but it is still preantral in this classification.
notes.D: Early antral follicles have a cavity that is still developing. A large dominant cavity characterises the mature stage.

questions.stem: The temporary endocrine gland formed from the follicle after ovulation is the:
questions.why: After follicular rupture, remaining granulosa and theca cells luteinise and form the corpus luteum. This temporary endocrine gland secretes progesterone to support the secretory endometrium.

notes.B: The corpus albicans is the fibrous scar left after the corpus luteum regresses. It is not the active postovulatory gland.
notes.C: An atretic follicle degenerates without completing the normal ovulatory sequence. It does not form a functioning postovulatory gland.
notes.D: A Graafian follicle is the mature preovulatory follicle. Luteinisation after rupture produces the temporary gland.
notes.E: Theca externa forms a supporting connective tissue layer around a follicle. The luteal steroid cells are derived mainly from granulosa and theca interna.

questions.stem: The main hormone produced by the corpus luteum is:
questions.why: The corpus luteum produces predominantly progesterone after ovulation, along with oestrogen. Its progesterone converts the oestrogen-primed endometrium into a secretory lining suitable for implantation.

notes.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone originates in anterior pituitary gonadotrophs and supports follicular development earlier in the cycle.
notes.C: Luteinising hormone is a pituitary signal that promotes luteinisation and supports luteal activity. The corpus luteum responds to it.
notes.D: Human chorionic gonadotrophin from trophoblast maintains luteal function in early pregnancy. It is not a major corpus luteum product.
notes.E: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone comes from hypothalamic neurons and regulates pituitary secretion upstream of the ovary.

questions.stem: Which process is completed in the oocyte shortly before ovulation?
questions.why: The preovulatory luteinising hormone surge promotes completion of meiosis I. This produces a secondary oocyte and a first polar body, with the secondary oocyte arresting again in meiosis II.

notes.B: Meiosis II reaches metaphase before ovulation but normally completes only after the secondary oocyte is activated by fertilisation.
notes.C: Oogonial mitosis belongs to fetal ovarian development. The growing preovulatory cell is already a meiotic oocyte.
notes.D: Fertilisation normally occurs in the uterine tube after ovulation releases the secondary oocyte from the follicle.
notes.E: Zona pellucida deposition starts in growing follicles well before the preovulatory resumption of meiosis.

questions.stem: At which stage is the oocyte arrested from fetal life until follicular maturation after puberty?

options.label: A
options.text: Prophase of the first meiotic division

options.label: B
options.text: Metaphase of the first meiotic division

options.label: C
options.text: Metaphase of the second meiotic division

options.label: D
options.text: Prophase of the second meiotic division

questions.why: A primary oocyte initiates meiosis during fetal life and pauses at diplotene of prophase I. This arrest can last for years until the follicle approaches ovulation.

notes.B: Metaphase I occurs after the primary oocyte resumes its first meiotic division near ovulation.
notes.C: Metaphase II is the later arrest of the ovulated secondary oocyte. The fetal arrest occurs during the first meiotic division.
notes.D: The long arrest is in prophase I. The secondary oocyte progresses into the second division only after meiosis I finishes.
notes.E: The oocyte has already entered meiosis by the time prolonged arrest begins. It does not remain in premeiotic interphase.

questions.stem: The glycoprotein layer that first separates follicular cells from the oocyte is the:
questions.why: The zona pellucida is an extracellular glycoprotein coat deposited around the growing oocyte. It lies between the oocyte surface and surrounding follicular cells and later participates in fertilisation.

notes.B: The corona radiata consists of living granulosa cells that lie just outside the zona pellucida.
notes.C: Theca interna is the steroidogenic layer outside the granulosa compartment. It is not the coat immediately surrounding the oocyte.
notes.D: A follicular basement membrane lies outside the granulosa layer, separating it from the theca rather than from the oocyte.
notes.E: The cumulus oophorus is a cluster of granulosa cells surrounding and attaching the oocyte to the follicle wall.

questions.stem: The granulosa cells that surround the oocyte and leave with it at ovulation form the:
questions.why: The corona radiata is the innermost layer of cumulus granulosa cells immediately external to the zona pellucida. These cells remain associated with the oocyte at ovulation.

notes.B: Theca interna lies outside the follicular basement membrane and supplies steroid precursors to granulosa cells.
notes.C: Theca externa is the outer supporting layer of the follicle. It is not carried away with the ovulated oocyte.
notes.D: Membrana granulosa denotes the granulosa lining of the follicle wall. The corona radiata is the specialised layer immediately surrounding the oocyte.
notes.E: The zona pellucida is an acellular glycoprotein coat. The surrounding cellular layer is made of granulosa cells.

questions.stem: A Forensic Scientist obtained sections of the ovary from an unknown female and tried to estimate the age of the female from the development of the ovarian follicles:

options.label: A
options.text: Ovaries of children usually show primordial follicles

options.label: B
options.text: Ovaries of sexually mature women show follicles at nearly all stages of development

options.label: C
options.text: Ovaries of postmenopausal women show only a few widely scattered follicles that have not developed

options.label: D
options.text: Postmenopausal ovaries have many remnants of corpora lutea and corpora albicantes

options.label: E
options.text: Ovaries of sexually mature women have more uni- and multilaminar follicles than antral follicles

notes.E: Many more early follicles than antral.

questions.why: All are true: a child's ovary shows mainly primordial follicles, the mature ovary shows follicles at all stages, and the postmenopausal ovary is small with only scattered follicles and corpora albicantia.

questions.stem: Gametogenesis in the female is called oogenesis and has ALL the following features EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Produces a single gamete per cycle

options.label: B
options.text: Female determines the genetic sex of the zygote

options.label: C
options.text: Continues until menopause when all oocytes are depleted

options.label: D
options.text: Arrested in fetal life and resumes at puberty

options.label: E
options.text: Meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs

questions.why: The sperm determines sex.

notes.A: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: True.
notes.E: True.

questions.stem: Analysis of semen from a spouse of an infertile marriage revealed normal number of spermatozoa with normal morphology but reduced motility. What is the correct terminology for this condition?
questions.why: Asthenozoospermia is reduced sperm motility. It can occur despite a normal sperm concentration and morphology because movement is a separate semen parameter.

notes.A: Aspermia means no semen is emitted. The stem describes an ejaculate that contains spermatozoa.
notes.B: Azoospermia means no sperm are identified in the ejaculate. Here sperm are present at a normal count.
notes.D: Oligozoospermia refers to a low sperm concentration. The abnormality described concerns the proportion of motile sperm.
notes.E: Teratozoospermia refers to an increased proportion of morphologically abnormal sperm. The given morphology is normal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is produced when the second meiotic division is completed in oogenesis?
questions.why: Fertilisation normally activates the secondary oocyte to complete meiosis II and extrude the second polar body. The retained maternal chromosomes then form the female pronucleus.

notes.B: An oogonium is an earlier mitotically dividing germ-cell precursor found during fetal ovarian development.
notes.C: A primary oocyte is present before completion of meiosis I and has the original diploid chromosome complement.
notes.D: The secondary oocyte is the product of meiosis I and is the cell that undergoes meiosis II.
notes.E: The retained haploid maternal chromosomes form the female pronucleus, which is explicitly included among the choices.

questions.stem: In spermatogenesis, in which cell do homologous chromosomes separate?
questions.why: Homologous chromosomes pair and then separate during meiosis I of the primary spermatocyte. Each daughter secondary spermatocyte receives one homolog from each pair, with sister chromatids still joined.

notes.A: Pale type A spermatogonia belong to the mitotic germ-cell population. They do not segregate homologous chromosome pairs in meiosis.
notes.B: Dark type A spermatogonia are undifferentiated germ cells. They precede the cells that undergo meiotic chromosome segregation.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are differentiating mitotic cells whose descendants enter meiosis as primary spermatocytes.
notes.E: A secondary spermatocyte already contains one chromosome from each homologous pair. It separates sister chromatids during meiosis II.

questions.stem: In spermatogenesis, in which cell do sister chromatids separate?
questions.why: In spermatogenesis the secondary spermatocyte enters meiosis II with duplicated chromosomes. Sister chromatids separate during that division to produce spermatids with unduplicated haploid chromosome sets.

notes.A: Pale type A spermatogonia can separate sister chromatids during ordinary mitosis. The context here is the meiotic stage of spermatogenesis.
notes.B: Dark type A cells are undifferentiated spermatogonia and are distinct from the cells performing the second meiotic division.
notes.C: Type B spermatogonia are mitotic precursors. Their descendants enter meiosis as primary spermatocytes.
notes.D: The primary spermatocyte separates homologous chromosomes in meiosis I. Sister chromatids stay joined until meiosis II.

questions.stem: Which is the gametogenic stem cell in the testis?
questions.why: Dark type A spermatogonia are the reserve stem cells; pale type A cells renew and commit to type B.

notes.A: Renewing, committed.
notes.C: Committed.
notes.D: In meiosis.
notes.E: In meiosis.

questions.stem: Spermatogenesis is harmed by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Spermatogenesis is sensitive to increased testicular temperature, ionising radiation, cytotoxic treatment and testicular inflammation. Migraine itself is not a recognised direct injury to the germinal epithelium.

notes.A: Normal core temperature is higher than the scrotal temperature favourable to spermatogenesis. Prolonged exposure to that heat can impair germ cells.
notes.B: Ionising radiation can damage dividing spermatogonia and related germ cells, reducing later sperm production.
notes.C: Antimitotic drugs can injure actively dividing germ cells and lower the output of the seminiferous epithelium.
notes.D: Mumps orchitis causes testicular inflammation and can impair spermatogenesis, especially when both testes are affected.

questions.stem: Which gamete provides the cytoplasm of the zygote?
questions.why: The oocyte supplies virtually all the zygote’s cytoplasm and most organelles, including the inherited mitochondrial population. The sperm provides paternal chromosomes and a small contribution of cellular components.

notes.B: The sperm contributes paternal DNA and factors involved in activation and early organisation. It supplies little cytoplasmic volume.
notes.C: Gametes contribute comparable haploid chromosome sets, but their cytoplasmic volumes are very different.
notes.D: The male pronucleus contains the paternal chromosome set. It is a nuclear structure within the oocyte-derived cytoplasm.
notes.E: The large oocyte supplies the cytoplasmic mass that sustains the early embryo before its own gene expression increases.

questions.stem: At which stage is oogenesis arrested from fetal life until puberty?
questions.why: Developing oocytes enter meiosis in fetal life and pause in the diplotene stage of prophase I. Selected oocytes resume that division in mature follicles after puberty.

notes.A: Anaphase I is when homologous chromosomes separate, after the prolonged prophase arrest has already been lifted.
notes.B: Metaphase II is the later arrest of the secondary oocyte near ovulation, usually lifted at fertilisation.
notes.D: Dictyotene is the prolonged diplotene stage of prophase I. It is not a subdivision of meiosis II.
notes.E: Leptotene is an early subdivision of prophase I. The prolonged fetal arrest occurs later, after homologues have paired.

questions.stem: Which cells secrete the oocyte maturation inhibitor responsible for meiotic arrest in oogenesis?
questions.why: Follicular granulosa cells help maintain prophase I arrest of the primary oocyte. Their signalling sustains oocyte cyclic nucleotide levels until luteinising hormone changes communication within the follicle.

notes.A: Primordial germ cells are early migratory precursors. The inhibitory signals arise from the somatic cells in the established follicle.
notes.B: Oogonia are fetal germ cells that proliferate before entering meiosis. They do not form the granulosa layer.
notes.C: Primary oocytes receive signals from their surrounding granulosa cells. Their own cyclic nucleotide pathways participate in the response.
notes.D: A secondary oocyte has already completed meiosis I. It pauses at metaphase II through a different arrest mechanism.

questions.stem: How long does the ovulated oocyte remain capable of fertilization?
questions.why: The ovulated secondary oocyte usually remains capable of fertilisation for roughly one day. It loses competence if sperm do not reach it during this relatively short interval.

notes.A: Three days exceeds the usual fertilisable life of the oocyte. Sperm can remain viable for several days in favourable conditions.
notes.C: One or two hours is too short for the usual oocyte interval. Fertilisation can occur later within the first day.
notes.D: Fourteen days approximates a typical luteal phase, which is far longer than postovulatory oocyte viability.
notes.E: Sixty-four days is measured on the scale of weeks and is unrelated to the brief fertilisable life of an ovulated oocyte.

questions.stem: Which of the statements below is NOT CORRECT concerning the male pronucleus?

options.label: A
options.text: Produced only after fertilization of ovum

options.label: B
options.text: Fuses with daughter cell of meiosis II of ovum

options.label: E
options.text: It is the polar body of meiosis II of the ovum

questions.why: The male pronucleus forms from the sperm head; polar bodies come from the oocyte.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: True.

questions.stem: In general, couples in which of the following ages are MOST FERTILE?
questions.why: Fertility is highest in the early twenties and declines with age.

notes.B: Slightly lower.
notes.C: Lower.
notes.D: Lower.
notes.E: Much lower.

questions.stem: What is the crucial role of the zona reaction in fertilization?

options.label: B
options.text: Stimulation of fusion of the pronuclei

questions.why: After fertilisation, oocyte cortical granules modify the zona pellucida and reduce further sperm entry. This contribution to the polyspermy block helps preserve the usual single paternal chromosome set.

notes.B: Pronuclear development occurs after gamete fusion. The zona modification is an extracellular defence against further sperm entry.
notes.C: Oocyte activation and intracellular calcium signalling promote completion of meiosis II. The zona change is a downstream response.
notes.D: The polyspermy block is correct. The added claim about stimulating pronuclear fusion does not describe the function of the zona reaction.
notes.E: The zona reaction restricts further sperm entry. Completion of meiosis II is triggered by activation of the oocyte.

questions.stem: The placenta forms from:
questions.why: The placenta has a fetal component formed by persistent villous chorion, the chorion frondosum, and a maternal component from decidua basalis beneath the implantation site.

notes.A: Decidua capsularis covers the conceptus toward the uterine cavity. The maternal placental bed is the decidua underneath it.
notes.B: Decidua basalis forms the maternal placental component. The fetal villous chorion supplies the other component.
notes.C: Chorion frondosum provides the fetal contribution with persistent branching villi. It develops in contact with maternal decidua basalis.
notes.D: Decidua basalis belongs to the placenta, but decidua capsularis covers the opposite side and does not supply the fetal villi.

questions.stem: How many oocytes result from the completion of maturation of a single oocyte in a primordial follicle?
questions.why: Unequal meiotic divisions conserve most cytoplasm in one functional oocyte. The other products are small polar bodies that contain expelled chromosome sets and do not become additional functional gametes.

notes.B: Meiosis I produces two unequal products. Only the larger daughter is a secondary oocyte, while the smaller daughter is a polar body.
notes.C: Polar bodies receive chromosomes and little cytoplasm. They therefore do not count as additional mature oocytes.
notes.D: Four functional haploid cells are characteristic of a completed spermatogenic lineage from one primary spermatocyte. Oogenesis retains one large gamete.
notes.E: A single functional cell is produced by normal maturation, so the resulting number is represented among the choices.

questions.stem: Which of the following are functions of Sertoli cells? i. Formation of the blood-testis barrier ii. They engineer the release of the late spermatids iii. Secretion of Androgen Binding Protein iv. Responsible for phagocytosis v. Secretion of testicular fluid
questions.why: Sertoli cells organise the seminiferous epithelium, form its barrier, and support and release developing germ cells. They secrete luminal fluid and androgen-binding protein and clear residual cytoplasm.

notes.A: The barrier and spermatid release are both supported by Sertoli cells. The selection omits secretion and phagocytic functions.
notes.B: The barrier, germ-cell release and androgen-binding protein are all relevant. Sertoli cells also clear residual material and provide fluid.
notes.C: Androgen-binding protein, phagocytosis and fluid production are included. The barrier and spermatid release also depend on Sertoli cells.
notes.D: The barrier, spermatid release and luminal fluid are correct. Androgen-binding protein secretion and phagocytosis are additional functions.

questions.stem: The average duration of gestation measured from the first day of the last normal menstrual period (LNMP) is

options.label: E
options.text: Determined by adding nine months to the first day of the LNMP

questions.why: Gestational age is conventionally counted from the first day of the last menstrual period. The expected duration is about 40 weeks, typically about 38 weeks from fertilisation.

notes.A: Thirty-four weeks is preterm in obstetric dating. It is shorter than the expected 40-week duration from the last menstrual period.
notes.B: About 38 weeks is the typical interval from fertilisation. Menstrual dating starts roughly two weeks earlier in a typical cycle.
notes.D: Forty-two completed weeks mark the usual threshold for post-term classification. They do not represent the average duration.
notes.E: Adding nine calendar months alone does not give the conventional 280-day estimate. Calendar months vary in length.

questions.stem: About oogenesis:

options.label: A
options.text: Primordial follicles hold primary oocytes arrested in prophase I

options.label: B
options.text: Primordial follicles do not undergo atresia

options.label: C
options.text: Primary follicles develop only after puberty

options.label: D
options.text: Antral follicle granulosa cells secrete oestrogen

options.label: F
options.text: A Graafian follicle holds an oocyte that has finished meiosis II

options.label: G
options.text: The ovulated gamete is a secondary oocyte

options.label: J
options.text: Usually only one follicle begins to mature each cycle

options.label: K
options.text: Usually only one follicle completes maturation each cycle

options.label: L
options.text: Oral contraceptives promote follicle growth but stop ovulation

notes.A: Primordial follicles enclose primary oocytes that have entered meiosis and arrested in prophase I.
notes.B: Primordial follicles can be lost from the ovarian reserve. Atresia also affects growing follicles throughout life.
notes.C: Early follicle growth can occur before puberty. Regular ovulatory cycles are established later.
notes.D: Granulosa cells aromatise theca-derived androgens to oestrogens as antral follicles develop.
notes.E: Most antral follicles contain primary oocytes. The secondary stage follows completion of meiosis I just before ovulation.
notes.F: The released oocyte normally pauses in metaphase II. Meiosis II is completed after activation by fertilisation.
notes.G: A secondary oocyte and associated cumulus cells leave the dominant follicle at ovulation.
notes.H: The mid-cycle luteinising hormone surge triggers ovulation. Follicle-stimulating hormone promotes follicular growth earlier.
notes.I: Oogonia proliferate and enter meiosis during fetal development, before the primordial follicle reserve is established.
notes.J: Several follicles can grow within a recruited cohort. Selection usually leaves one dominant follicle.
notes.K: Usually one dominant follicle reaches ovulation. The other recruited follicles commonly undergo atresia.
notes.L: Combined oral contraceptives generally suppress gonadotrophin-dependent follicular development and the ovulatory surge. They do not promote maturation.

questions.why: Primary oocytes enter meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I. A cyclic cohort can grow, but usually one dominant follicle releases a secondary oocyte after the luteinising hormone surge.

questions.stem: In Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) a conceptus is introduced into the uterus of a hormonally stimulated female at which stage of development?
questions.why: In IVF the cleaving embryo is usually transferred at about the 8-cell stage (day 3) or as a blastocyst.

notes.A: Too early.
notes.B: Possible, but usually later.
notes.D: Morula; not the usual transfer stage.
notes.E: Usually blastocyst by then.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the reason for the hormones contained in the female contraceptive pill?

options.label: C
options.text: Stimulation of zona reaction of ovum before sperms reach it

options.label: D
options.text: Suppression of hypothalamic secretion of gonadotrophin releasing hormone

options.label: E
options.text: Suppression of female orgasm during coitus

questions.why: Combined oral contraceptive steroids exert negative feedback on the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis. Reduced gonadotrophin stimulation and suppression of the luteinising hormone surge help prevent ovulation.

notes.A: Withdrawal bleeding can still occur during a hormone-free interval. Ovulation suppression is the principal mechanism targeted by this choice.
notes.B: Changes in cervical mucus can impede sperm passage. The pill does not act by directly blocking the sperm acrosome reaction.
notes.C: The zona reaction follows oocyte activation after fertilisation. Oral contraceptive hormones act upstream to reduce the chance of ovulation.
notes.E: Orgasm is not a target of oral contraceptive action. The relevant hormonal effects involve the reproductive endocrine axis.

questions.stem: The embryonic process that involves morphogenetic movement of cells is:
questions.why: During gastrulation, epiblast cells move through the primitive streak and take up new positions. These coordinated movements establish the three germ layers and the embryonic body plan.

notes.A: Implantation attaches the blastocyst to endometrium and includes trophoblast invasion. The germ-layer-forming movements are a distinct embryonic event.
notes.B: Fertilisation unites the gametes and activates the oocyte. It precedes the later redistribution of epiblast cells.
notes.C: The acrosomal reaction involves changes in the sperm head that help it interact with the oocyte’s extracellular coverings.
notes.D: Decidualisation is differentiation of maternal endometrial stroma, not rearrangement of embryonic epiblast into germ layers.

questions.stem: Which process blocks polyspermy?
questions.why: After oocyte activation, cortical granules modify the zona pellucida around the oocyte. This reduces further sperm binding and penetration and contributes to the block to polyspermy.

notes.A: Nidation means implantation in the endometrium and occurs after cleavage, several days after fertilisation.
notes.C: Capacitation prepares sperm for fertilisation through membrane and signalling changes. It acts before the polyspermy block.
notes.D: Acrosomal exocytosis is a sperm event that assists fertilisation. The zona modification is an oocyte response after activation.
notes.E: Ejaculation releases semen into the reproductive tract. It does not modify the egg coat after a sperm enters.

questions.stem: Events that may give rise to a hydatidiform mole include:

options.label: A
options.text: Fertilization of an ovum by more than one spermatozoon

options.label: B
options.text: Failure of the ovum to encounter a competent spermatozoon

options.label: C
options.text: Fertilization of more than one ovum at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of the zygote to expel the secondary polar body

options.label: E
options.text: Expulsion of the male or female pronucleus after fertilization

notes.B: No conceptus.
notes.C: Gives twins.
notes.D: Gives triploidy, not a mole.

questions.why: Partial mole: two sperm fertilize an ovum. Complete mole: a sperm fertilizes an "empty" ovum (no maternal nucleus).

questions.stem: The “morning after” emergency contraceptive pill works by delivering a large dose of oestrogen within 72 hours of coitus. Which of the following explains how it works?

options.label: A
options.text: If an ovulation has not recently occurred, it prevents the ovum from being released

options.label: B
options.text: If an ovum has been released, its fertilization may be impaired

options.label: C
options.text: If fertilization has already occurred, implantation is inhibited

options.label: D
options.text: Cleavage division and production of the blastocyst is adversely affected

questions.why: Emergency contraception can delay or inhibit ovulation, alter tubal transport and make the endometrium unreceptive, so all the listed mechanisms apply.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True.
notes.D: True.

questions.stem: All of the following are reasons for permitting emergency contraceptive use, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: A couple who plan for a baby may change their mind

options.label: B
options.text: Condoms being used for contraception may tear

options.label: C
options.text: Women on contraceptive pills may forget to take them

options.label: E
options.text: Coitus may be forced as in rape or incest

questions.why: Emergency contraception is justified for genuine failures or assault; a couple simply changing their mind about a planned pregnancy is not a recognised indication, so it is the exception.

notes.B: Valid.
notes.C: Valid.
notes.D: Valid.
notes.E: Valid.

questions.stem: Which of the following terminologies refer to the condition of an adult male whose ejaculate contains very few spermatozoa?
questions.why: Oligozoospermia means a low concentration of spermatozoa in semen. It describes a measurable semen parameter without specifying the cause or establishing whether conception is possible.

notes.A: Azoospermia means no sperm are found in the ejaculate. In this stem, a small number of sperm are present.
notes.C: Infertility is a broader clinical diagnosis. A low sperm concentration is one possible contributor and has its own term.
notes.D: Erectile dysfunction describes difficulty attaining or maintaining an erection. It does not specify the sperm count in semen.
notes.E: The semen finding has a specific name. The other terms describe absence of sperm, broader fertility status or erectile function.

questions.stem: Female factors that account for infertility includes of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: All of these can cause female infertility.

notes.A: Cause.
notes.B: Hostile to sperm.
notes.C: Cause.
notes.D: Cause.

questions.stem: Although none has been carried out in humans yet, which type of cloning is ethically and morally less objectionable in terms of human development?
questions.why: Therapeutic cloning makes cells or tissues, not a new person.

notes.A: Makes individuals.
notes.B: Makes individuals.
notes.D: One is less objectionable.
notes.E: Not all.

questions.stem: Which type of cloning technique was used in the recent achievement of growing whole heart valves from embryonic stem cells?
questions.why: Growing tissues or organs from embryonic stem cells for transplantation is therapeutic (biomedical) cloning, as distinct from reproductive cloning.

notes.B: Makes whole animals.
notes.C: Splits embryos.
notes.D: Only one.
notes.E: One is correct.

questions.stem: Binding of the sperm head to the ovum during fertilization is facilitated by which of the following?
questions.why: Zona pellucida glycoproteins help sperm interact with the oocyte’s outer coat. ZP3 is involved in classical models, while evidence in humans also supports important roles for other zona proteins.

notes.A: Hyaluronidase contributes to passage through the hyaluronan-rich cumulus matrix. It is not an egg-coat recognition glycoprotein.
notes.B: Acrosin is an acrosomal protease involved during sperm passage. The zona glycoprotein provides the proposed interaction site.
notes.C: Neuraminidase acts on terminal sialic acid residues. It is not the zona glycoprotein implicated in this sperm-binding choice.
notes.E: The zona reaction is the alteration of the coat after oocyte activation, which reduces further sperm interaction.

questions.stem: Capacitation of spermatozoa involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Removal of glycoproteins from the membrane covering the acrosome

options.label: B
options.text: Perforations in the membrane covering the acrosome

options.label: C
options.text: Release of proteases from the acrosome

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of the acrosomal cap to expose the sperm head

questions.why: Capacitation involves changes to the sperm plasma membrane, including loss or rearrangement of surface components. These changes prime sperm for hyperactivated motility and a later acrosomal reaction.

notes.B: Membrane fusion and vesiculation are features of the later acrosomal reaction. Capacitation prepares the sperm to undergo it.
notes.C: Proteases are released during acrosomal exocytosis. Capacitation is a preparatory process before that release.
notes.D: Acrosomal cap changes occur with acrosomal exocytosis, after the sperm has acquired competence to respond.
notes.E: The sperm retains its flagellum during capacitation. Signalling changes help it move with a hyperactivated motility pattern.

questions.stem: The following are structural changes that accompany follicle development EXCEPT
questions.why: Growing follicles increase in size, gain granulosa cells and develop the zona pellucida and antrum. The theca interna differentiates and supports steroid production during the growing stages.

notes.A: As antral follicles mature, follicular fluid accumulates and the cavity enlarges, displacing the oocyte towards the edge.
notes.B: The size of the follicle increases with granulosa growth, thecal differentiation and later accumulation of follicular fluid.
notes.D: Proliferation of granulosa cells expands the layer surrounding the oocyte and later the wall around the antrum.
notes.E: The zona pellucida appears around the growing oocyte as an extracellular glycoprotein layer.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes in fertilization trigger(s) the zonal reaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Fusion of plasma membranes of oocyte and sperm head

options.label: B
options.text: Binding of signaling molecules in corona radiata to acrosomal membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Release of paternal chromosomes in sperm head to form male pronucleus

questions.why: Fusion of the sperm and oocyte membranes initiates oocyte activation and intracellular calcium signals. Cortical granule release then modifies the zona pellucida to limit further sperm entry.

notes.B: Interactions with the cumulus can influence sperm behaviour, but cortical granule release follows activation within the oocyte.
notes.C: Passage through the corona radiata occurs before the sperm reaches the oocyte membrane and before the cortical response.
notes.D: A sperm first passes through the zona pellucida. Oocyte activation follows fusion with the oocyte membrane beyond the zona.
notes.E: The male pronucleus forms after activation and cortical granule exocytosis have already begun.

questions.stem: Recurring problems with in vitro fertilization (IVF) include:

options.label: A
options.text: Legal battles over ownership of embryos following divorce

questions.why: IVF carries risks including multiple pregnancy, ovarian hyperstimulation and low implantation/success rates, so all the listed problems apply.

notes.A: A problem.
notes.B: A problem.
notes.C: A problem.
notes.D: A problem.

questions.stem: The removal of glycoproteins from the membrane over the acrosome, exposing receptor sites, is called:
questions.why: Capacitation remodels the sperm plasma membrane and signalling pathways after ejaculation. Loss or rearrangement of surface material over the acrosome helps prepare sperm for fertilisation.

notes.A: The zona reaction modifies the oocyte’s glycoprotein coat after activation. It occurs in a different cell at a later stage.
notes.B: Flagellar motion propels sperm. Membrane remodelling may change the beat pattern but is the specific process named here.
notes.C: Spermiation is release of elongated spermatids from Sertoli cells into the seminiferous tubule lumen, before epididymal passage.
notes.D: Physiological maturation is a broad description. Capacitation is the specific post-ejaculatory change to fertilising competence asked for here.

questions.stem: Which method of contraception is NOT recommended for a young person who has had no children?
questions.why: Sterilization is effectively permanent, so it is not advised for young people with no children.

notes.B: Reversible.
notes.C: Reversible.
notes.D: Reversible.
notes.E: One is not recommended.

questions.stem: Which method of contraception is 100% effective?
questions.why: Each listed contraceptive method has a nonzero failure rate. Effectiveness varies both with the method and with how consistently and correctly it is used.

notes.A: Condoms can break, slip or be used inconsistently. These possibilities leave a measurable pregnancy risk.
notes.B: Hormonal pills are highly effective when used correctly. Missed doses and other factors can reduce real-world effectiveness.
notes.C: Calendar methods estimate fertile days. Ovulation timing varies, so pregnancy remains possible even when users track cycles.
notes.D: Spermicides used alone have a measurable failure rate, with effectiveness depending in part on correct timing and application.

questions.stem: With which of the listed parts is the spermatozoon self-propelled?
questions.why: The flagellum produces bending waves that propel the sperm. Its axonemal motor proteins generate movement, while metabolic pathways including those in the midpiece supply energy.

notes.A: The acrosome is a cap on the sperm head containing substances involved in fertilisation. It does not generate thrust.
notes.B: The head carries the condensed paternal genome and acrosome. Forward propulsion is produced by movement of the flagellum.
notes.C: The neck contains connecting structures linking the head to the flagellum. The propulsive beat runs along the flagellum.
notes.D: The midpiece contains a mitochondrial sheath and part of the flagellar apparatus. The flagellum as a whole provides propulsion.

questions.stem: Two years after bilateral orchidectomy, a man has a semen analysis. The likely finding is:
questions.why: Removal of both testes eliminates the source of spermatozoa. If an ejaculate is produced later, it contains no sperm because accessory glands contribute fluid but cannot make germ cells.

notes.A: Aspermia is absence of an ejaculate. When fluid is obtained for analysis, absence of sperm is recorded separately.
notes.B: Globozoospermia describes abnormal round-headed sperm. There must be sperm present for this morphological finding.
notes.C: Oligozoospermia denotes a low sperm concentration with some sperm remaining. With no testes, new sperm are not produced.
notes.E: Hypospermia describes reduced semen volume. The expected sperm-specific finding after bilateral testis removal is absence of sperm.

questions.stem: Which method of contraception depends on charting the menstrual cycle?
questions.why: The rhythm or calendar method uses previous menstrual cycle lengths to estimate the fertile window. Contraceptive use depends on avoiding unprotected intercourse during the predicted fertile days.

notes.A: An intrauterine device prevents pregnancy through its actions within the reproductive tract. Routine use does not require cycle charting.
notes.B: Barrier methods physically reduce sperm passage during intercourse. Their action does not depend on predicting ovulation.
notes.D: Hormonal methods act through reproductive hormone signalling or cervical mucus changes. They are not defined by calendar tracking.
notes.E: Withdrawal requires removing the penis before ejaculation. It does not identify fertile days from the menstrual cycle.

questions.stem: Injectable or implantable contraceptives fall under which broad method of contraception?
questions.why: Contraceptive injections and implants deliver hormones that can suppress ovulation or thicken cervical mucus. Progestogens are typical, and some injectable formulations also contain oestrogen.

notes.B: A barrier physically blocks sperm. Injections and implants instead deliver a drug whose contraceptive action is hormonal.
notes.C: Implants are removable and injections wear off with time. They are intended to be reversible methods.
notes.D: Calendar methods estimate the fertile window from cycle patterns. These contraceptives act whether or not cycles are charted.
notes.E: An intrauterine device sits inside the uterus. An implant is placed under the skin and an injection is administered separately.

questions.stem: Which of the following are classified as permanent methods of contraception?
questions.why: Tubal sterilisation and vasectomy interrupt reproductive ducts and are intended as permanent contraception. A contraceptive implant provides long-acting hormonal contraception and can be removed.

notes.A: Tubal ligation or occlusion is a permanent method. The choice omits vasectomy, which is also intended to be permanent.
notes.B: Vasectomy interrupts sperm transport through the ductus deferens and is intended to be permanent. Tubal sterilisation also qualifies.
notes.C: The implant releases a hormone for a limited duration and can be removed when the user wants to discontinue it.
notes.D: The surgical methods meet the permanent category. The implant is a long-acting reversible method, so including it makes this combination incorrect.

questions.stem: What is released during the acrosome reaction?
questions.why: During the acrosome reaction, membranes at the anterior sperm head fuse and vesiculate. Acrosomal enzymes are released and help the sperm interact with the oocyte’s coverings.

notes.B: The acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes rather than a hormone-secreting system. Exocytosis releases its enzymatic contents.
notes.C: Acrosomal membranes are remodelled and can shed vesicles. The characteristic released soluble contents asked for are enzymes.
notes.D: Enzyme release is correct, but the additional claim of hormone release is not part of acrosomal exocytosis.
notes.E: This combination includes hormone release and omits the enzymatic contents characteristically released from the acrosome.

questions.stem: About how many days after fertilization does implantation begin?
questions.why: Implantation usually starts about six to seven days after fertilisation. By then a hatched blastocyst can appose and attach to receptive secretory endometrium.

notes.A: At one to two days, cleavage is under way while the early embryo is still moving along the uterine tube.
notes.B: Around days two to three the embryo has several blastomeres. The enclosing zona is still usually present.
notes.C: Compaction and early blastocyst formation occur around this period. Endometrial attachment usually begins after hatching.
notes.E: By ten to twelve days implantation is usually well advanced. The first attachment takes place several days sooner.

questions.stem: About IVF (assisted conception):

options.label: A
options.text: A woman with both tubes blocked is a good candidate

options.label: B
options.text: A woman with both ovaries removed needs donor eggs

options.label: C
options.text: A woman with no uterus does not need a surrogate

options.label: D
options.text: A man with no sperm in his semen can never use his own sperm

options.label: E
options.text: A man with a low sperm count can use his own sperm

options.label: F
options.text: A man after vasectomy can use his own sperm

options.label: G
options.text: A man with a blocked urethra cannot use his own sperm

options.label: H
options.text: Frozen sperm can be thawed and used

options.label: I
options.text: Sperm do not undergo the acrosome reaction in IVF

options.label: J
options.text: A postmenopausal surrogate needs no hormone treatment

notes.A: IVF brings sperm and oocytes together outside the body. Embryo transfer bypasses the blocked uterine tubes.
notes.B: Bilateral ovary removal eliminates new oocyte retrieval. Donor oocytes are needed if the patient has no previously stored oocytes or embryos.
notes.C: A person without a functional uterus cannot carry an intrauterine pregnancy. A gestational carrier can carry the transferred embryo.
notes.D: Some causes of azoospermia allow sperm retrieval from the testis or epididymis, depending on the cause and extent of sperm production.
notes.E: A low sperm count does not necessarily prevent using the patient’s sperm. Laboratory techniques can help when viable sperm are available.
notes.F: Vasectomy blocks the ductus deferens rather than sperm production. In selected cases, sperm can be retrieved for assisted fertilisation.
notes.G: A urethral obstruction can prevent semen delivery. Selected patients may have sperm retrieved upstream if spermatogenesis is intact.
notes.H: Cryopreserved sperm can be thawed and assessed for use in assisted reproduction if sufficient viable cells remain.
notes.I: Sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction in conventional IVF. Direct intracytoplasmic injection bypasses its usual role in zona penetration.
notes.J: A postmenopausal endometrium generally needs hormonal preparation for embryo transfer because it lacks the usual cyclic ovarian support.

questions.why: In vitro fertilisation can bypass obstructed tubes and can use retrieved, stored or donated gametes. Embryo transfer also requires a receptive uterus, which can be hormonally prepared.

questions.stem: Direct consequences of fertilization include:

options.label: D
options.text: completion of the first meiotic division

options.label: E
options.text: completion of the second meiotic division of the oocyte

notes.A: Oocyte activation releases cortical granules that modify the zona pellucida and limit additional sperm entry.
notes.B: The fertilising sperm usually contributes either an X or a Y chromosome, establishing the zygote’s sex chromosome complement.
notes.C: The acrosome reaction occurs in the sperm before membrane fusion and helps enable interaction with the oocyte’s extracellular coverings.
notes.D: Meiosis I normally finishes just before ovulation. Fertilisation activates completion of the second meiotic division.
notes.E: Activation allows the metaphase II-arrested oocyte to separate sister chromatids and extrude its second polar body.
notes.F: Oocyte activation initiates development leading to cleavage, the mitotic division sequence of the new embryo.
notes.G: The fusion and activation events establish the fertilised single cell known as the zygote.
notes.H: Formation of a blastocyst requires several days of cleavage and organisation after the zygote has formed.
notes.I: Combining independently assorted and recombined maternal and paternal genomes creates a new genetic combination in the zygote.
notes.J: The second polar body is expelled. The maternal chromosome set retained in the oocyte forms the female pronucleus.

questions.why: Sperm–oocyte fusion activates the secondary oocyte, modifies its coat and completes meiosis II. Combining the parental genomes establishes the zygote and enables the first cleavage divisions.

questions.stem: Conditions that can prevent successful intercourse or the availability of competent gametes:

options.label: A
options.text: one undescended testis at 3 months of age

options.label: F
options.text: failure of the man to ejaculate

options.label: G
options.text: failure of the woman to have an orgasm

options.label: M
options.text: gonorrhoeal blockage of the ejaculatory ducts

options.label: N
options.text: TB blocking the urethra in a woman

notes.A: An undescended testis in infancy needs follow-up, but this finding alone does not establish adult infertility, particularly if the other testis is normal.
notes.B: Pelvic infection can scar the uterine tubes, preventing gametes from meeting or impairing embryo transport.
notes.C: Genital infection can alter secretions or cause inflammation that impairs sperm passage. General vaginal acidity alone is not a diagnosis.
notes.D: Erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction can prevent effective deposition of semen even when sperm production is intact.
notes.E: Severe obesity can affect ovulation and other reproductive functions through endocrine and metabolic mechanisms.
notes.F: Absent ejaculation can prevent sperm delivery to the female reproductive tract even if sperm are produced.
notes.G: Female orgasm is not required for sperm deposition, fertilisation or normal implantation.
notes.H: An obstructed vaginal outlet can prevent penetrative intercourse or access to the cervix, depending on the anatomy.
notes.I: A single length threshold does not determine whether intercourse or semen deposition is possible.
notes.J: Kartagener syndrome is a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia. It can impair sperm flagellar motility.
notes.K: Fallopian tube ciliary dysfunction can impair gamete or embryo transport in those with primary ciliary dyskinesia.
notes.L: Abnormally thick or poorly penetrable cervical mucus can impede sperm passage, although clinically significant cervical-factor infertility is uncommon.
notes.M: Ductal scarring can obstruct delivery of sperm from the male reproductive tract into the urethra.
notes.N: The female urethra is a urinary passage. Obstruction there is not itself a blockage of the sperm or oocyte route.

questions.why: Infertility can reflect problems with intercourse, delivery or function of gametes, and passage through reproductive ducts. Clinical effect depends on the specific site, severity and associated findings.

questions.stem: About cloning of mammals:

options.label: A
options.text: Clones have the same nuclear DNA as the donor

options.label: B
options.text: Blastomeres at the 4-cell stage can give 4 clones

options.label: C
options.text: Blastomeres at the 16-cell stage can give 16 clones

options.label: D
options.text: Only totipotent cells can be used

options.label: F
options.text: Natural identical twins are more perfect clones

options.label: G
options.text: Clones from nuclear transfer have different cytoplasm from their parent

options.label: H
options.text: Clones carried in successive pregnancies have different uterine environments

notes.A: Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg.
notes.B: Totipotent.
notes.C: No longer totipotent.
notes.D: Somatic nuclei can be reprogrammed (Dolly).

questions.why: Clones share the donor's nuclear DNA, early (e.g. 4-cell) blastomeres can each form an individual, surrogates are needed, natural identical twins are more perfect clones, and nuclear-transfer clones carry the recipient egg's cytoplasm (A, B, E-H true); C is false (16-cell blastomeres are no longer totipotent) and D is false (somatic-cell nuclear transfer uses differentiated, not only totipotent, nuclei).

questions.stem: Which is the first layer that differentiates from the embryoblast?
questions.why: The embryoblast separates into epiblast and hypoblast. The hypoblast is the early layer called primitive endoderm, which contributes to yolk-sac lining rather than the definitive embryonic gut.

notes.A: The amnion develops around the early amniotic cavity adjacent to the epiblast. It is a membrane rather than the primitive endodermal layer.
notes.B: The chorion combines trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. It does not arise as the first embryoblast layer.
notes.D: Definitive embryonic ectoderm is derived from the epiblast during gastrulation, after the bilaminar disc has formed.
notes.E: Intraembryonic mesoderm forms when epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak during gastrulation.

questions.stem: After implantation, which embryonic tissue is in direct contact with maternal tissue (endometrium)?
questions.why: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated trophoblast layer at early implantation. It penetrates the endometrium and forms the early interface with surrounding maternal tissue.

notes.A: The embryoblast is the inner cell mass that forms the embryonic disc. Maternal contact is made by the overlying trophoblast.
notes.B: The amniotic membrane surrounds the forming cavity next to the epiblast. It lies within the conceptus.
notes.C: The primary yolk sac forms toward the hypoblast inside the conceptus. It is not the invasive maternal interface.
notes.D: Cytotrophoblast is the inner cellular trophoblast layer that supplies cells to the overlying syncytium during initial implantation.

questions.stem: Which of the following arises directly from embryoblast?
questions.why: The embryoblast, or inner cell mass, gives rise to the epiblast and hypoblast. These layers form the early bilaminar embryonic disc before the primitive streak develops.

notes.B: Trophoblast derives from the outer cells of the early blastocyst, whereas the embryoblast is its inner cell population.
notes.C: Extraembryonic mesoderm develops later around embryonic cavities. It is not one of the initial layers formed directly by segregation of the embryoblast.
notes.D: Intraembryonic mesoderm comes from epiblast cells passing through the primitive streak during gastrulation, after the bilaminar disc stage.
notes.E: The epiblast is a direct derivative of the embryoblast and is included among the choices.

questions.stem: At which stage of development does implantation occur?
questions.why: Implantation begins when the blastocyst hatches and attaches to receptive endometrium. Its outer trophoblast then differentiates and invades the uterine lining.

notes.A: The zygote is the single cell immediately after fertilisation and is still in the uterine tube at this stage.
notes.B: A sixteen-cell embryo is usually at or approaching the morula stage, before the blastocyst forms and hatches.
notes.C: Cell number alone does not define readiness for implantation. A cavitated, hatched blastocyst attaches through its trophoblast.
notes.E: The bilaminar disc describes differentiation within the embryoblast during early implantation. The whole conceptus attaches as a blastocyst.

questions.stem: Which of the following events is decisive for initiation of implantation?
questions.why: Loss of the zona pellucida lets the blastocyst’s trophoblast contact the receptive endometrium directly. This hatching step enables the apposition and adhesion that start implantation.

notes.B: Endometrial decidual changes support implantation. Hatching is the immediate physical prerequisite that exposes the trophoblast for contact.
notes.C: The inner and outer cell populations segregate earlier as the blastocyst forms. The surrounding coat still has to be shed.
notes.D: The other processes contribute to development or uterine response, but neither substitutes for exposing the trophoblast by hatching.
notes.E: Zona shedding opens access to the endometrial surface, so a recognised prerequisite is present among the choices.

questions.stem: Which phase of development is the endometrium in at the commencement of implantation?
questions.why: The blastocyst attaches during the postovulatory secretory phase. Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrial glands secretory and helps establish a receptive implantation window.

notes.A: The proliferative phase precedes ovulation and is driven mainly by oestrogen. Implantation usually starts after the luteal phase begins.
notes.B: Decidualisation can begin in the secretory phase and intensifies around implantation. Secretory is the cycle phase asked for here.
notes.D: The postovulatory secretory phase is a standard term and is included among the choices.
notes.E: The endometrium is not in every listed phase. Progesterone-dependent secretory maturation precedes attachment.

questions.stem: Which decidua in NOT in direct contact with any trophoblast throughout embryonic development?
questions.why: The decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterus; it never touches trophoblast directly.

notes.A: Over the conceptus.
notes.C: Under it.
notes.D: Only one.
notes.E: One is correct.

questions.stem: Splitting of the embryo can give identical twins at the:

notes.A: Separation of the inner embryonic population at the blastocyst stage is classically associated with a shared chorion.
notes.B: Very early cleavage-stage separation can produce two separate blastocysts with their own chorions and amnions.
notes.C: Cells can also separate at the morula stage, before a single chorion has been established.
notes.D: The conventional model places ordinary complete twinning earlier. Very late incomplete separation is sometimes invoked to explain conjoined twinning.
notes.E: Neurulation follows early axis formation and is well beyond the usual time assigned to separation into two embryos.

questions.why: Monozygotic twins form when one early conceptus separates into two embryonic lineages. In the classical model, the time of separation influences which fetal membranes are shared.

questions.stem: Which is the commonest site of ectopic implantation?
questions.why: Most ectopic pregnancies implant in a uterine tube, particularly its ampullary region. Tubal implantation occurs before the blastocyst reaches the usual site in the uterine cavity.

notes.A: Cervical implantation is a recognised but uncommon form of ectopic pregnancy. Tubal locations are substantially more frequent.
notes.B: The ovary can be an ectopic implantation site, but ovarian pregnancies account for a small minority of ectopic pregnancies.
notes.C: An abdominal implant occurs outside the uterine cavity and tube. It is less frequent than tubal implantation.
notes.E: The uterine tube is the most common ectopic site, and it appears explicitly among the options.

questions.stem: Which are the first cells to differentiate from the morula?
questions.why: As the morula compacts, outer cells adopt trophectoderm identity and inner cells form the embryoblast. The outer lineage supplies the trophoblast of the developing blastocyst.

notes.A: The amnion forms later around the cavity adjacent to the epiblast, after the primary outer and inner lineages separate.
notes.B: The chorion is a membrane formed later from trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm.
notes.C: The hypoblast separates later within the inner cell mass. It is not the early outer lineage of the morula.
notes.D: The epiblast is specified within the embryoblast after the outer trophectoderm lineage is established.

questions.stem: The term for the changes the endometrium undergoes in response to implantation is:
questions.why: Decidualisation is the progesterone-responsive transformation of endometrial stromal cells. It begins during the secretory phase and becomes more pronounced around the implanting conceptus.

notes.A: Capacitation alters sperm membranes and signalling during preparation for fertilisation. It does not describe an endometrial change.
notes.B: Gastrulation reorganises the embryonic epiblast into germ layers. Decidualisation occurs in maternal tissue.
notes.D: Nidation is implantation itself. The associated stromal transformation of the uterine lining is a separate process.
notes.E: Fertilisation unites sperm and oocyte and normally occurs in the uterine tube, before the endometrial response.

questions.stem: What are the cells produced by cleavage of the zygote called?
questions.why: Cleavage divides the zygote mitotically into smaller cells without corresponding overall growth. These individual cells are blastomeres, which later compact and contribute to blastocyst lineages.

notes.A: A blastocyst is the entire later structure containing a cavity and specialised cell populations. Individual cleavage cells have a different name.
notes.C: Trophoblast cells belong to an outer lineage established after early cleavage and compaction. The earlier cells are blastomeres.
notes.D: The embryoblast is the inner cell mass in the blastocyst. It represents one population descended from blastomeres.
notes.E: Only one term describes the individual products of cleavage. The other terms refer to later structures or lineages.

questions.stem: Implantation at which site gives rise to placenta praevia?
questions.why: Low uterine implantation can leave the placenta near the internal cervical opening. Placenta praevia is diagnosed when placental tissue overlies that opening later in pregnancy.

notes.A: Tubal implantation is an ectopic pregnancy. Placenta praevia concerns placental location in a pregnancy within the uterus.
notes.C: Fundal implantation is high in the uterus and usually places the placenta away from the internal cervical opening.
notes.D: Ovarian implantation is an ectopic pregnancy and cannot produce the usual placental relationship to the cervical opening.
notes.E: Abdominal implantation is ectopic. The relationship defining placenta praevia occurs within the lower uterus.

questions.stem: Which of the following results from fusion of the male and female pronuclei?
questions.why: Fertilisation establishes a single-cell zygote containing maternal and paternal chromosome sets. Its pronuclear envelopes later break down so the chromosomes can participate in the first mitosis.

notes.A: The first polar body is produced when the primary oocyte completes meiosis I. It forms before the paternal genome enters.
notes.B: The second polar body results from completion of meiosis II after activation. It does not retain both parental genomes.
notes.C: A pronucleus contains one parental chromosome set before the first zygotic mitosis. The whole fertilised cell is the zygote.
notes.E: A blastomere is produced when the zygote starts cleavage. It is a daughter cell rather than the initial fertilised cell.

questions.stem: The syncytiotrophoblast:

options.label: B
options.text: Gives rise to the decidua basalis

options.label: C
options.text: Begins to develop on the 4th day after fertilization

options.label: D
options.text: Is derived from the zona pellucida

options.label: E
options.text: Degenerates once cytotrophoblast takes over its function

questions.why: The syncytiotrophoblast secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin after implantation begins. The hormone maintains the early corpus luteum and thereby sustains progesterone production until placental production increases.

notes.B: Decidua basalis is maternal endometrial tissue beneath the implant. The syncytiotrophoblast contributes to the fetal placental component.
notes.C: Around day four the conceptus is usually at the morula or early blastocyst transition. Invasive syncytium appears with implantation.
notes.D: The zona pellucida is the surrounding glycoprotein coat that is shed before implantation. Syncytiotrophoblast is derived from trophoblast.
notes.E: The villous syncytiotrophoblast remains present and provides an exchange and endocrine surface. Cytotrophoblast cells replenish it by fusion.

questions.stem: Fraternal (dizygotic) twins:

options.label: E
options.text: may come from two oocytes from the same ovary

options.label: F
options.text: may come from oocytes from both ovaries

options.label: G
options.text: may be of the same sex

notes.A: Each oocyte is fertilised separately, so there are two zygotes rather than separation of one zygote.
notes.B: Dizygotic twins are genetically comparable to other full siblings. Each inherits a different combination of parental alleles.
notes.C: Two adjacent placental discs can join and appear as one mass, while the pregnancy remains dichorionic.
notes.D: Dizygotic twins ordinarily form separate amniotic sacs because they originate from two separate conceptuses.
notes.E: Two oocytes may be released from follicles in the same ovary within one ovulatory cycle.
notes.F: Ovulatory follicles in both ovaries can release oocytes that are subsequently fertilised in the same cycle.
notes.G: The two fertilisations are independent. The twins can have the same or different sex chromosome complements.
notes.H: Each fetus has its own umbilical cord, even when the outer placental discs are fused.

questions.why: Dizygotic twins arise when two separate oocytes are fertilised. Each twin usually has a separate chorion, amnion and cord, although adjacent placental discs can fuse.

questions.stem: Identical (monozygotic) twins:

options.label: A
options.text: may come from two secondary oocytes

notes.E: If splitting is late.
notes.H: Each has its own unless conjoined.

questions.why: Identical twins come from one fertilised ovum, are genetically identical, are always the same sex, and depending on timing may share a placenta or even an amniotic cavity (B-F true); A, G and H are false (they arise from a single oocyte, are monozygotic not dizygotic, and usually have separate umbilical cords).

questions.stem: About implantation:

options.label: A
options.text: The zona pellucida breaks down after implantation

options.label: C
options.text: Attachment occurs at the embryonic pole

options.label: D
options.text: Early on, the decidua capsularis lies between conceptus and myometrium

options.label: E
options.text: Early on, the decidua basalis covers the conceptus toward the uterine cavity

options.label: F
options.text: The chorion laeve forms against the decidua capsularis

options.label: G
options.text: The chorion frondosum forms against the decidua parietalis

options.label: H
options.text: The endometrium is secretory at implantation

options.label: I
options.text: After implantation the endometrium becomes proliferative

options.label: J
options.text: The syncytiotrophoblast is in direct contact with maternal tissue

notes.A: The zona pellucida is shed before attachment, exposing the trophoblast so it can contact the endometrial surface.
notes.B: The morula is an earlier solid cell mass. Implantation begins after blastocyst formation and hatching.
notes.C: Attachment usually begins on the side of the blastocyst containing the embryoblast, known as the embryonic pole.
notes.D: Decidua basalis lies deep to the conceptus toward the myometrium. Capsularis covers the opposite side.
notes.E: Decidua capsularis faces the uterine cavity. Decidua basalis lies beneath the site of implantation.
notes.F: Villi regress on the capsular side, producing smooth chorion, or chorion laeve, against the decidua capsularis.
notes.G: Branching villi persist at the maternal placental bed, which is decidua basalis rather than the parietal lining.
notes.H: Implantation begins in progesterone-conditioned secretory endometrium during the postovulatory phase.
notes.I: The endometrium undergoes further decidual change after attachment. It does not return to its preovulatory proliferative state.
notes.J: Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer invasive layer and directly contacts surrounding maternal tissue at the implantation site.

questions.why: A hatched blastocyst attaches at its embryonic pole to secretory endometrium. Trophoblast invades at that site, where persistent villi form the chorion frondosum against decidua basalis.

questions.stem: Which mesoderm contributes to the formation of the amniotic membrane in an embryo?
questions.why: The amnion includes amniotic epithelium with a supporting outer layer of extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. This layer is also called somatopleuric mesoderm.
